name: Ahanta Kingdom
description: The Ahanta Kingdom was an Akan coastal state flourishing along the southwestern littoral of modern Ghana. Organised as a confederation of regional chiefdoms under a paramount ruler at Busua, the realm grew prosperous through maritime commerce and controlled vital trading posts frequented by Dutch and British merchants. It retained political autonomy until mounting British imperial intervention in the nineteenth century gradually curtailed its sovereign authority. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Busua; Common languages: Ahanta and Akan; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional confederacy; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1840; Succeeded by: British Gold Coast

name: Aich-Ai
description: Aich-Ai was an indigenous pastoral chiefdom established by Nama communities in the arid terrain of southern Namibia. Operating from its base at Aich-Ai, the polity regulated vital desert pastures, seasonal waterholes and regional livestock trade across the Great Fish River basin. It retained its independence through collective local governance until German colonial authorities annexed the surrounding territory into German South West Africa in 1886. \n\n Status: Indigenous chiefdom; Capital: Aich-Ai; Common languages: Khoekhoe; Religion: Traditional beliefs; Government: Chieftaincy; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 8 January 1886; Succeeded by: German South West Africa

name: Alawi Sheikhdom
label: southern arabia petty kingdoms
description: The Alawi Sheikhdom was an autonomous tribal polity located in the rugged Aden hinterland of southwestern Yemen. Centred upon the fortified settlement of Al-Qash'ah, the realm commanded strategically vital caravan tracks traversing the Tuban Valley and maintained its independence under hereditary Alawi sheikhs. This sovereign period concluded on 16 July 1895 when its ruler concluded a formal protectorate treaty with the British Empire. \n\n Status: Sheikhdom; Capital: Al-Qash'ah; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary tribal sheikhdom; Historical era: Modern era; Reorganised: 16 July 1895; Succeeded by: Aden Protectorate

name: AmaPondomise
description: AmaPondomise was an independent South African kingdom of the Mpondomise people occupying the fertile hill country of the upper Mzimvubu basin. Ruled from the royal seat at Tsolo, the realm preserved its distinct cultural institutions and cattle-rearing economy while resisting regional turbulence during the Mfecane and expanding European colonial frontiers. The monarchy's sovereignty ended on 22 November 1872 following voluntary cession and administrative incorporation into the British Cape Colony. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Tsolo; Common languages: Mpondomise and Xhosa; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 22 November 1872; Succeeded by: Cape Colony

name: Amarro
description: Amarro was an autonomous Omotic kingdom situated across the Amaro highlands to the east of Lake Chamo in southwestern Ethiopia. Nestled among naturally defensible mountain ridges, the state maintained a thriving terraced agricultural system under local hereditary rulers who retained independence from neighbouring Oromo groups. Its long-standing autonomy concluded in 1891 when the expansionist armies of Emperor Menelik II conquered and incorporated the region into the Ethiopian Empire. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Amarro; Common languages: Koorete; Religion: Traditional beliefs; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Awing
description: Awing was a traditional Grassfields fondom established in the highlands of northwestern Cameroon. Governed by a paramount fon alongside sacred regulatory societies, the kingdom maintained extensive agricultural terraces and participated in dynamic regional trade networks connecting the Bamenda plateau. It preserved complete domestic sovereignty throughout the nineteenth century until German colonial expeditions subjugated the territory into German Kamerun in 1901. \n\n Status: Fondom; Capital: Awing; Common languages: Awing and Ngemba; Religion: Traditional beliefs; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Fon; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Bakong
description: Bakong was an independent precolonial chiefdom located across the lush Bamileke highlands of western Cameroon. The polity was governed by an indigenous sovereign assisted by council elders, sustaining an agrarian economy based on root crops and regional trade across the volcanic plateaux. The community successfully retained its autonomy until the opening years of the twentieth century, when German military advances absorbed the territory into the colonial protectorate of Kamerun. \n\n Status: Traditional chieftaincy; Capital: Bakong; Common languages: Bamileke; Religion: Traditional beliefs; Government: Chieftaincy; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Bambui
description: Bambui was a prosperous Grassfields fondom located in the fertile Tubah valley of modern northwestern Cameroon. Sheltered by the Sabga hills, the kingdom developed highly productive farming systems and served as a crucial crossroad for inter-community commerce and cultural exchange across the Bamenda region. The fondom remained fully self-governing until 1901, when imperial German forces asserted colonial dominion over the surrounding highlands. \n\n Status: Fondom; Capital: Bambui; Common languages: Bambui; Religion: Traditional beliefs; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Fon; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Bassar
description: Bassar was a renowned precolonial chiefdom and metalworking centre located in the savanna hills of northern Togo. Celebrated across West Africa for its sophisticated iron smelting industry and extensive furnace complexes, the realm dominated regional metallurgical trade routes between the Volta basin and the interior. The chiefdom maintained its independence until 1896, when German imperial forces annexed the territory into the protectorate of Togoland. \n\n Status: Traditional chiefdom; Capital: Bassar; Common languages: Bassar; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Chieftaincy; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1896; Succeeded by: German Togoland

name: Baté Empire
description: The Baté Empire was an influential Islamic commercial state centred upon the historic metropolis of Kankan in upper Guinea. Established by Mandinka and Soninke clerical families, the state derived immense prosperity from trans-Saharan commerce, gold trading and its prestige as a foremost centre of Islamic scholarship. Its long era of sovereign governance ended in 1880 when the military forces of Samori Ture conquered Kankan and incorporated it into the Wassoulou Empire. \n\n Status: Islamic merchant state; Capital: Kankan; Common languages: Mandinka and Soninke; Religion: Islam; Government: Theocratic merchant state; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1880; Succeeded by: Wassoulou Empire

name: BaTswana
description: The BaTswana polity was an autonomous federation of Tswana-speaking chiefdoms occupying the vast savanna lands between the Molopo River and the Kalahari margins. Governed by hereditary kgosi ruling from central settlements such as Molepolole, the state directed extensive cattle pastoralism and communal assemblies known as kgotla. The confederacy maintained sovereign control over its ancestral territories until 1886, when British authorities partitioned the region into the Bechuanaland Protectorate and British Bechuanaland. \n\n Status: Traditional confederacy; Capital: Molepolole; Common languages: Setswana; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Confederacy of chieftaincies; Ruler title: Kgosi; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: Bechuanaland Protectorate

name: Bolama
description: Bolama was a contentious British colonial outpost established on the mangrove-fringed island of the same name off the coast of Portuguese Guinea. Founded initially as an experimental agricultural and anti-slavery settlement, the enclave remained precariously garrisoned by British commercial interests while enduring harsh tropical illnesses and persistent territorial disputes with the Kingdom of Portugal. British jurisdictional claims waned after 1838, culminating decades later in formal international arbitration that confirmed Portuguese sovereignty. \n\n Status: Colony of Great Britain; Capital: Bolama; Common languages: English and Portuguese Creole; Religion: Christianity; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1838; Succeeded by: Portuguese Guinea

name: Bramaya
description: Bramaya was an independent precolonial coastal kingdom situated along the Rio Pongo basin in lower Guinea. Governing fertile alluvial plains and estuarine mangrove networks, the realm derived revenue from local agriculture, salt manufacturing and maritime trade with European and African merchants. The kingdom retained its traditional monarchy until 1892, when French colonial forces systematically subdued the coastal chieftaincies and annexed Bramaya into French Guinea. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Bramaya; Common languages: Susu; Religion: Traditional beliefs and Islam; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1892; Succeeded by: French Guinea

name: Buhavu
description: Buhavu was a precolonial kingdom of the Havu people located along the western shores and islands of Lake Kivu in the eastern Congo basin. Led by a divine monarch known as the Kami, the state developed an intricate feudal hierarchy supported by intensive banana cultivation, fishing and lacustrine commerce. It preserved its sovereignty against regional rivals until 1 November 1885, when European powers at the Berlin Conference assigned the Kivu basin to the Congo Free State. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Katana; Common languages: Havu; Religion: Traditional beliefs; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Kami; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1 November 1885; Succeeded by: Congo Free State

name: Buyungu
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Buyungu was an autonomous precolonial kingdom situated in the rugged Great Lakes plateau of northwestern Tanzania. Ruled by a traditional hereditary sovereign, the polity commanded highland agricultural slopes and trade tracks linking Lake Victoria with the central caravan corridors. The kingdom successfully maintained its political cohesion until 1891, when German imperial forces annexed the surrounding chiefdoms into German East Africa. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Buyungu; Common languages: Ha; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: German East Africa

name: Chomba
description: Chomba was an independent Grassfields polity located amidst the rocky, precipitous hills of the Bamenda highlands in western Cameroon. Inhabited primarily by the Ngemba people, the community maintained a rugged agrarian lifestyle centred upon terraced subsistence farming and pastoral grazing along the high ridges. Chomba preserved its ancestral independence through tight-knit local governance until German colonial expeditions penetrated and subdued the highlands in 1901. \n\n Status: Traditional polity; Capital: Chomba; Common languages: Ngemba; Religion: Traditional beliefs; Government: Chieftaincy; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Corisco
description: Corisco was an autonomous island chiefdom established by the Benga people on Corisco Island at the mouth of the Muni River estuary. Positioned strategically on the Gulf of Guinea, the kingdom flourished as a vital commercial emporium where Benga seafaring merchants brokered lucrative trade between inland populations and visiting European vessels. Its sovereign independence endured until 1859, when escalating Spanish commercial pressure resulted in the formal establishment of a Spanish colonial protectorate. \n\n Status: Island chiefdom; Capital: Corisco; Common languages: Benga; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1859; Succeeded by: Spanish Guinea

name: Dathina Sheikhdom
label: southern arabia petty kingdoms
description: The Dathina Sheikhdom was an independent tribal confederation situated across the arid plateau northeast of Aden in southwestern Arabia. Administered through a council of tribal elders and sheikhs based at Mudiyah, the state regulated strategic caravan corridors connecting the southern Arabian coastline with the interior highlands. It preserved complete autonomy throughout the nineteenth century until it was formally incorporated into the British Aden Protectorate network. \n\n Status: Sheikhdom; Capital: Mudiyah; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Tribal confederation; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: Aden Protectorate

name: Dubréka
description: Dubréka was an autonomous coastal chieftaincy established by the Susu and Baga peoples along the tidal creeks immediately north of the Kaloum Peninsula in lower Guinea. Governing fertile coastal wetlands and mangrove estuaries, the community thrived by managing salt production, rice agriculture and maritime trade with European merchant vessels. The polity retained its independence until 1851, when expanding French military influence brought the surrounding littoral under colonial treaties. \n\n Status: Traditional chiefdom; Capital: Dubreka; Common languages: Susu and Baga; Religion: Traditional beliefs and Islam; Government: Chieftaincy; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1851; Succeeded by: French Guinea

name: Efron
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: Efron was a sovereign Yoruba city-kingdom located in the undulating hill country of modern Ekiti State in southwestern Nigeria. Led by a sacred traditional monarch, the polity maintained fortified defensive works, rich agricultural holdings and active participation in the regional commerce of the eastern Yoruba interior. The kingdom preserved its autonomy through the tumultuous nineteenth-century Yoruba wars until British colonial authorities annexed the district into the Lagos Protectorate in 1894. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Efron; Common languages: Yoruba; Religion: Yoruba religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Oba; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1894; Succeeded by: Lagos Protectorate

name: Emirate of Dhala
label: southern arabia petty kingdoms
description: The Emirate of Dhala, also known as the Amiri state, was an independent highland realm positioned along the mountainous trade routes of southwestern Arabia. Ruled by a hereditary emir from the fortress town of Ad Dali, the state zealously defended its mountain passes and agricultural valleys against Ottoman incursions and regional competitors. It maintained autonomous status across two distinct nineteenth-century periods before formal British treaty arrangements firmly established protectorate oversight. \n\n Status: Emirate; Capital: Ad Dali; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Modern era; Reorganised: 1881; Succeeded by: Aden Protectorate

name: Esu
description: Esu was a sovereign precolonial chiefdom situated in the mountainous Grassfields region of northwestern Cameroon. Governed by a traditional fon supported by elder lineages, the polity maintained terraced farms in the highland valleys and engaged in regional barter trade with neighbouring communities. Its independent existence continued unbroken until 1901, when imperial German colonial troops subjugated the indigenous societies of the Bamenda highlands. \n\n Status: Traditional chiefdom; Capital: Esu; Common languages: Esu; Religion: Traditional beliefs; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Fon; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Eyumodjock and Ossing
description: Eyumodjock and Ossing was an autonomous Ejagham polity located in the dense equatorial rainforests of the Manyu river basin in western Cameroon. Governed through communal councils and the influential Ekpe leopard society, the community controlled vital rainforest trade routes and harvested forest goods for coastal exchange. The polity maintained its ancestral independence until 1901, when imperial German forces advanced into the Cross River hinterland and annexed the region into Kamerun. \n\n Status: Traditional polity; Capital: Eyumodjock; Common languages: Ejagham; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Council of elders; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Fika
description: Fika was a powerful precolonial kingdom established by the Bole people in the savanna country of northeastern Nigeria. Governed by the hereditary Moi of Fika from a heavily fortified earthen capital, the state resisted Fulani jihadist conquest and preserved its indigenous cultural traditions, cavalry forces and political institutions. The kingdom retained sovereign independence until 27 December 1899, when British imperial forces conquered the territory and established colonial administration. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Fika; Common languages: Bole and Hausa; Religion: Traditional beliefs and Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Moi; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 27 December 1899; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Gciriku
description: Gciriku was an autonomous precolonial kingdom of the Kavango people situated along the northern banks and floodplains of the Okavango River in northeastern Namibia. Governed by a traditional monarch known as the Hompa from the royal seat at Nyangana, the realm developed a prosperous mixed economy based on riverine fishing, cattle keeping and floodplain agriculture. The kingdom sustained its domestic sovereignty until 1896, when German colonial authorities established formal imperial control over the Kavango region. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Nyangana; Common languages: Rumanyo; Religion: Traditional beliefs; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Hompa; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1896; Succeeded by: German South West Africa

name: Gwalior State
label: indian princely states
description: Gwalior State was a premier Maratha princely state located in Central India, ruled by the illustrious Scindia dynasty from the fortified city of Gwalior. Having emerged as a formidable military power under Mahadji Scindia, the state entered into subsidiary alliance with the British East India Company in the early nineteenth century while retaining internal administrative autonomy and enjoying a twenty-one gun salute. It endured as one of the wealthiest and most prominent states in the Indian Empire until signing the instrument of accession to the Dominion of India on 15 June 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state of the British Raj; Capital: Gwalior; Common languages: Hindi and Marathi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Autocratic monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Scindia; Ruler title: Maharaja Scindia; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 15 June 1948; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Hawshabi Sultanate of Musaymir
label: southern arabia petty kingdoms
description: The Hawshabi Sultanate of Musaymir was an autonomous South Arabian principality located in the rugged mountainous corridor northwest of Aden. Governed by hereditary Hawshabi sultans from the capital of Musaymir, the polity controlled critical caravan trails passing through the Tuban basin and levied transit duties on commercial traffic between Sana'a and the coast. Its period of unencumbered sovereignty concluded on 14 June 1839 following the British capture of Aden and subsequent protective treaty arrangements. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Musaymir; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary sultanate; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Modern era; Reorganised: 14 June 1839; Succeeded by: Aden Protectorate

name: Ikirun
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: Ikirun was a prominent precolonial Yoruba kingdom and garrison town situated in the fertile interior of modern Osun State in southwestern Nigeria. Governed by the Akirun of Ikirun, the polity served as a pivotal military bulwark protecting the northern Yoruba frontier and engaged in extensive regional warfare, notably during the Jalumi War of 1878. The city-state retained its autonomy until 1891, when British colonial forces pacified the warring Yoruba kingdoms and established imperial oversight. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Ikirun; Common languages: Yoruba; Religion: Yoruba religion and Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Akirun; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: Lagos Protectorate

name: Ikungu
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Ikungu was an independent precolonial chiefdom situated on the dry savannah plateau of central Tanzania. Governed by a traditional hereditary ruler, the polity sustained an agro-pastoral economy and commanded key local pathways linked to the central long-distance caravan trade between the Swahili coast and Lake Tanganyika. The chiefdom maintained its autonomous status until 1891, when imperial German forces consolidated colonial rule across German East Africa. \n\n Status: Traditional chiefdom; Capital: Ikungu; Common languages: Nyamwezi; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Chieftaincy; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: German East Africa

name: Ilaro
description: Ilaro was an autonomous Yoruba kingdom and the premier cultural capital of the Yewa people in southwestern Nigeria. Established in the eighteenth century by migratory warriors from Oyo, the realm flourished as a vital agricultural and trading hub producing cocoa, kola nuts and maize while preserving celebrated Gelede masquerade traditions. The kingdom maintained sovereign governance until 13 August 1891, when its leaders signed a treaty placing Ilaro under the protection of the British Crown Colony of Lagos. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Ilaro; Common languages: Yoruba; Religion: Yoruba religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Olu of Ilaro; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 13 August 1891; Succeeded by: Lagos Protectorate

name: Ilorin Emirate
label: hausa states
description: The Ilorin Emirate was a powerful northern frontier state established in southwestern Nigeria following the secession of Afonja from the Oyo Empire and subsequent incorporation into the Sokoto Caliphate. Ruled by an Islamic emir of Fulani lineage from the bustling capital of Ilorin, the emirate blended Yoruba culture with Islamic governance and maintained a formidable cavalry army. It functioned as an independent caliphal state until 1898, when forces of the Royal Niger Company conquered the city and established British colonial dominance. \n\n Status: Emirate; Capital: Ilorin; Common languages: Yoruba, Fulfulde and Hausa; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1898; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Jath State
label: indian princely states
description: Jath State was a non-salute Maratha princely state located on the Deccan plateau in modern southern Maharashtra. Founded in the late seventeenth century as a hereditary jagir under the Bijapur Agency, the state was ruled by the Hindu Patil dynasty of Daphlapur and entered into formal subsidiary ties with the British East India Company. It remained a self-governing dependency of the Bombay Presidency until its formal merger into the newly independent Dominion of India in 1949. \n\n Status: Princely state of the British Raj; Capital: Jath; Common languages: Marathi and Kannada; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1949; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Kabu
description: Kabu was an autonomous Bassar and Gur-speaking chiefdom situated in the hilly savanna of northern Togo. Governed by a hereditary chief from its central fortified village, the community maintained self-sufficient agricultural terracing and took part in the celebrated regional iron smelting and forging trade that linked central Togo to neighbouring markets. The polity defended its independence against regional invasions until 1896, when German imperial troops occupied the region and incorporated it into Togoland. \n\n Status: Traditional chiefdom; Capital: Kansala; Common languages: Bassar and Kabye; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Chieftaincy; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1896; Succeeded by: German Togoland

name: Kahare
description: Kahare was an independent precolonial kingdom of the Nkoya people situated across the woodlands of the Kasempa district in north-central Zambia. Governed by a revered traditional ruler bearing the dynastic title of Kahare, the state practiced shifting cultivation and controlled local hunting grounds and trade routes across the Kafue river system. The realm preserved its domestic independence until the 1890s, when expanding Lozi hegemony and British South Africa Company expeditions brought the area under colonial control. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Kahare; Common languages: Nkoya; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Mwene Kahare; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: British South Africa Company

name: Karenni States
label: shan states
description: The Karenni States formed an autonomous confederacy of mountainous Red Karen principalities located along the rugged frontier between British Burma and Siam. Ruled by traditional saophas from valley settlements, the confederation zealously preserved its independence through formal diplomacy, including an 1875 treaty in which Britain and the Burmese kingdom mutually recognised Karenni sovereignty. This sovereign autonomy endured until 1893, when British authorities extended political supervision over the states without fully incorporating them into British Burma. \n\n Status: Traditional confederacy; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Karenni; Religion: Traditional beliefs; Government: Confederacy of principalities; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Modern era; Reorganised: 1893; Succeeded by: Federated Shan States

name: Kengcheng State
label: shan states
description: Kengcheng State, also known as Chiang Khaeng, was a Tai Lue tributary principality situated along the upper Mekong River valley between modern Myanmar and Laos. Governed by a hereditary saopha residing at Kengcheng, the realm managed riverine ferry crossings and fertile rice basins while rendering formal vassal homage and tribute to the Konbaung monarchs of Burma. This tributary arrangement continued until 1886, when British forces toppled the Burmese monarchy and subsequently partitioned the territory between British Burma and French Indochina. \n\n Status: Vassal state of Burma; Capital: Kengcheng; Common languages: Tai Lue and Shan; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Kibosho
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Kibosho was a powerful sovereign Chagga kingdom established on the fertile southwestern slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro in modern Tanzania. Governed by a paramount monarch styled the Mangi from his fortified palace compound, the state constructed extensive irrigation canals, defensive trenches and banana groves while fielding disciplined war bands. Kibosho maintained complete political independence under renowned rulers until 1891, when German imperial forces subjugated the Kilimanjaro kingdoms into German East Africa. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Kibosho; Common languages: Kikibosho and Chagga; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Mangi; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: German East Africa

name: Kingdom of Bugisu
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Bugisu was an autonomous precolonial polity of the Gisu people located around the fertile volcanic slopes of Mount Elgon in eastern Uganda. Ruled from the regional centre of Mbale, the society was structured around clan networks and age-set systems that managed terraced agriculture, coffee cultivation and vital montane trade routes. The state preserved its independence until 1901, when military campaigns led by Semei Kakungulu integrated Bugisu into the British Uganda Protectorate. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Mbale; Common languages: Masaaba; Religion: Traditional beliefs; Government: Chieftaincy; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: Uganda Protectorate

name: Kingdom of Bukedi
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Bukedi was an independent precolonial realm situated on the undulating plains of eastern Uganda near the foot of Mount Elgon. Governed from Tororo, the polity comprised diverse ethnic communities that maintained mixed agro-pastoral lifestyles, millet farming and regional commerce across the Great Lakes interior. It retained its traditional autonomy throughout the nineteenth century until British colonial forces and allied Baganda troops subjugated the district into the Uganda Protectorate in 1901. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Tororo; Common languages: Dhopadhola and Ateso; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: Uganda Protectorate

name: Kingdom of Buzinza
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Buzinza was an autonomous Great Lakes realm located along the southwestern shores of Lake Victoria in modern Tanzania. Governed by a hereditary omukama from Geita, the kingdom prospered through iron mining, smithing traditions and long-distance commerce connecting interlacustrine kingdoms with Swahili caravans. Its period of sovereign independence ended on 1 July 1890 under the terms of the Anglo-German Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty, which incorporated the territory into German East Africa. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Geita; Common languages: Zinza; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Omukama; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1 July 1890; Succeeded by: German East Africa

name: Kingdom of Gomma
label: kingdoms in the gibe region
description: The Kingdom of Gomma was an autonomous Muslim state established in the fertile Gibe region of southwestern Ethiopia. Centred at Agaro, the kingdom was governed by a hereditary monarch who embraced Sunni Islam in the early nineteenth century and promoted intensive coffee cultivation, civet farming and highland commerce. Gomma defended its sovereignty against neighbouring Oromo states until 1887, when the imperial armies of Menelik II conquered and incorporated it into the Ethiopian Empire. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Agaro; Common languages: Oromo; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1887; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Kingdom of Jeypore
label: indian princely states
description: The Kingdom of Jeypore was an expansive zamindari princely realm situated across the Eastern Ghats in southern Odisha. Tracing its royal lineage to the fifteenth century, the state was ruled by the Hindu Suryavanshi kings from Jeypore and maintained substantial internal autonomy under the British Madras Presidency following subsidiary agreements. The principality preserved its rich tribal heritage, judicial authority and palace administration until its formal accession and integration into independent India in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state of the British Raj; Capital: Jeypore; Common languages: Odia; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Suryavanshi; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Kingdom of Kiga
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Kiga was an independent precolonial polity of the Bakiga people occupying the steep terraced hills of Kigezi in southwestern Uganda. Headed from Kabale through federated clan councils and spiritual leaders, the community fiercely repelled outside incursions while cultivating sorghum and maintaining resilient mountain agricultural systems. The realm preserved its independence from neighbouring kingdoms until 1901, when British imperial forces and colonial agents gradually annexed Kigezi into the Uganda Protectorate. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Kabale; Common languages: Rukiga; Religion: Traditional beliefs; Government: Clan-based monarchy; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: Uganda Protectorate

name: Kingdom of Lagos
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Lagos was an influential maritime Yoruba realm situated around the lagoon islands and sand spits of the Bight of Benin. Initially founded under the suzerainty of the Benin Empire, the city-state established factual autonomy by the early nineteenth century and derived substantial commercial wealth as an Atlantic trading hub. Its independence concluded on 6 August 1861 when Oba Dosunmu ceded the territory to the British Crown under the Lagos Treaty of Cession. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Lagos; Common languages: Yoruba; Religion: Yoruba religion and Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Oba; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 6 August 1861; Succeeded by: Lagos Colony

name: Kingdom of Nagpur
description: The Kingdom of Nagpur was a sovereign Maratha state governed by the Bhonsle dynasty across the expansive plateaux of central and eastern India. Centred upon the city of Nagpur, the realm maintained powerful cavalry armies, collected chauth across surrounding regions and played an assertive role in the Maratha Confederacy. Its sovereign status came to an end on 9 January 1818 following defeat in the Third Anglo-Maratha War, after which it was reduced to a subsidiary princely state. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Nagpur; Common languages: Marathi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bhonsle; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 9 January 1818; Succeeded by: Nagpur State

name: Kingdom of Rapa
description: The Kingdom of Rapa was an isolated Polynesian realm established on the mountainous island of Rapa Iti in the Bass Islands. Governed by a traditional ariki residing at Ahurei, the insular community maintained fortified ridge villages and intensive taro terrace farming while sustaining unique genealogical traditions. name: Sultanate of Maradi

Governed by a traditional monarch titled the Omukama from the Bahinda dynasty, the polity established an organised agrarian society supported by extensive banana cultivation and cattle herding. Promulgating its constitution in April 1811 under President Jorge Tadeo Lozano and later Antonio Nariño, the state declared autonomy while resisting the loose federalist model favoured by neighbouring provinces. name: Republic of Paraguay

Under the leadership of José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia and later the López dynasty, the state pursued economic self-sufficiency, social stability and formidable military mobilisation. name: States of Venezuela
description: The States of Venezuela, historically known as the First Republic of Venezuela, was a pioneering sovereign confederation established following the formal declaration of independence from Spain on 5 July 1811. Adopting a federal constitution that abolished noble privileges and trade monopolies, the fledgling government established its administrative seat at Valencia under a rotating triumvirate and later Generalissimo Francisco de Miranda. Beset by royalist counter-attacks, economic inflation and the catastrophic 1812 Caracas earthquake, the republic collapsed with the capitulation of San Mateo in July 1812. \n\n Status: Sovereign federal republic; Capital: Valencia; Common languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Federal republic; Head of state: Francisco de Miranda; Historical era: Spanish American wars of independence; Established: 5 July 1811; Disestablished: 25 July 1812; Preceded by: Captaincy General of Venezuela; Succeeded by: Captaincy General of Venezuela

name: Free State of Cartagena
description: The Free State of Cartagena was an autonomous revolutionary republic declared on 11 November 1811 when civic leaders and popular militias in Cartagena de Indias proclaimed absolute independence from the Spanish crown. Becoming the first territory in New Granada to formally sever all constitutional ties with the Bourbon monarchy, the coastal state established its own legislative body and maritime defences. Its brief sovereign isolation concluded after sixteen days when Cartagena's representatives ratified the federal pact creating the United Provinces of New Granada. \n\n Status: Revolutionary city-state; Capital: Cartagena de Indias; Common languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Constitutional republic; Historical era: Spanish American wars of independence; Established: 11 November 1811; Disestablished: 27 November 1811; Preceded by: Viceroyalty of New Granada; Succeeded by: United Provinces of New Granada

name: United Provinces of New Granada
description: The United Provinces of New Granada was a federal republic established on 27 November 1811 by rebel provinces seeking coordinated self-government in the wake of the Spanish imperial collapse. Operating from Tunja and subsequently Santafé de Bogotá, the federation functioned under a parliamentary constitution with a collective presidency and a powerful representative congress. The republic struggled with ideological divisions during the Patria Boba before succumbing to a devastating Spanish counter-offensive led by General Pablo Morillo in July 1816. \n\n Status: Sovereign federal republic; Capital: Santafé de Bogotá; Common languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Federal republic; Currency: Real; Historical era: Spanish American wars of independence; Established: 27 November 1811; Disestablished: 10 July 1816; Preceded by: Viceroyalty of New Granada; Succeeded by: Viceroyalty of New Granada

name: District of Assiniboia
description: The District of Assiniboia, also known as the Red River Colony, was a British settlement colony founded in 1812 by Thomas Douglas, 5th Earl of Selkirk, on land granted by the Hudson's Bay Company. Spanning the Red and Assiniboine river valleys across modern southern Manitoba and neighbouring borderlands, the colony became a vibrant homeland for Scottish settlers, Métis hunters and French-Canadian canoemen. Administered from Upper Fort Garry, the territory retained chartered colonial governance until its formal incorporation into the Dominion of Canada as Manitoba in 1870. \n\n Status: British proprietary colony; Capital: Upper Fort Garry; Common languages: English, French, Cree and Saulteaux; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Presbyterianism; Government: Proprietary colonial administration; Head of state: Governor; Historical era: Canadian Confederation; Established: 1812; Disestablished: 15 July 1870; Succeeded by: Canada

name: Jama'are Emirate
label: fula jihads polities
description: Jama'are Emirate was an autonomous Islamic state located in the savanna lands of modern northern Bauchi State, Nigeria. Established around 1812 by Fulani pastoralist clans from the Lake Chad basin under the leadership of Muhammadu Wabi I, the emirate emerged during the wider Sokoto jihad as a regional religious and administrative centre. Governed from the walled town of Jama'are, the emirate maintained its domestic autonomy and traditional dynastic institutions until British imperial forces subordinated the realm to the Northern Nigeria Protectorate in November 1903. \n\n Status: Sovereign Islamic emirate; Capital: Jama'are; Common languages: Fulfulde and Hausa; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Precolonial West Africa; Established: 1812; Disestablished: 1 November 1903; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Jamkhandi State
label: indian princely states
description: Jamkhandi State was a Maratha princely principality located in the Deccan region of southern Maharashtra and northern Karnataka. Founded in 1811 by the Patwardhan Chitpavan Brahmin family following the fragmentation of the Peshwa's territories, the realm accepted British paramountcy under the Deccan States Agency. Governed from its capital at Jamkhandi along the Krishna River basin, the rajas promoted irrigation, modern education and civic amenities until signing the instrument of accession to the Indian Union in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state of British India; Capital: Jamkhandi; Common languages: Marathi and Kannada; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Patwardhan; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1811; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Kenghkam State
label: shan states
description: Kenghkam State was a minor tributary Shan principality located along the Nam Pang River valley in the southern Shan hills of eastern Burma. Acknowledging the suzerainty of the Burmese Konbaung monarchy, the local Shan chieftains remitted regular levies and pledged allegiance to the royal court at Mandalay. The state was administered from the riverine settlement of Keng Hkam, maintaining traditional feudal traditions until dynastic strife and regional reorganisation led to its annexation by the neighbouring principality of Möng Nai. \n\n Status: Tributary state of the Konbaung Kingdom; Capital: Kenghkam; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary chieftaincy; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Late Konbaung period; Established: 1812; Disestablished: 1879; Preceded by: Konbaung dynasty; Succeeded by: Möng Nai

name: Kurundvad State
label: indian princely states
description: Kurundvad State was a Maratha princely principality situated in the Deccan plateau along the banks of the Panchganga River. Founded in the eighteenth century by the Patwardhan dynasty under the Maratha Empire, the state came under British paramountcy in 1812 within the Deccan States Agency of the Bombay Presidency. Administered from the town of Kurundvad in modern Kolhapur district, the principality's scattered enclaves were partitioned between senior and junior family branches until both lines acceded to independent India in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state of British India; Capital: Kurundvad; Common languages: Marathi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely state; Ruling dynasty: Patwardhan; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1733; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Maluka State
description: Maluka State was a short-lived private principality established in south-eastern Borneo around the Maluka River basin near Banjarmasin. Created in 1812 through a land concession granted by the Sultan of Banjar to the English merchant adventurer Alexander Hare, the domain was governed with sovereign pretensions supported by recruited Javanese labourers and private guards. Operating from its headquarters at Bati-Bati, the settlement functioned as an autonomous plantation estate until restored Dutch colonial authorities dismantled Hare's administration and annexed the territory in 1817. \n\n Status: Autonomous proprietary estate; Capital: Bati-Bati; Common languages: English, Malay and Javanese; Religion: Christianity and Sunni Islam; Government: Autocratic proprietary monarchy; Head of state: Alexander Hare; Ruler title: Rajah; Historical era: British East Indies interregnum; Established: 1812; Disestablished: 1817; Preceded by: Sultanate of Banjar; Succeeded by: Dutch East Indies

name: Orchha State
label: indian princely states
description: Orchha State was a premier fifteen-gun salute princely realm located in the Bundelkhand region of central India, governed by the senior branch of the Bundela Rajput dynasty. Entering into protective treaty relations with the British East India Company in 1812, the state formed the nucleus of the Bundelkhand Agency while preserving extensive feudal autonomy. The maharajas ruled from the historic citadel of Orchha and later Tikamgarh, patronising classical architecture and religious shrines until acceding to the Indian Union in 1950. \n\n Status: Princely state of British India; Capital: Orchha; Common languages: Hindi and Bundeli; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely state; Ruling dynasty: Bundela; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1501; Disestablished: 1950; Succeeded by: Republic of India

name: Nawanagar State
label: indian princely states
description: Nawanagar State was a prominent thirteen-gun salute maritime princely kingdom situated along the southern shores of the Gulf of Kutch in modern Gujarat. Founded in 1540 by the Jadeja Rajput dynasty, the state entered into subsidiary alliance with the British on 22 February 1812 within the Kathiawar Agency. Governed from its capital at Jamnagar, the realm prospered from pearl fisheries, textile manufacture and Arabian Sea commerce until merging into the United State of Kathiawar in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state of British India; Capital: Jamnagar; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism, Islam and Jainism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jadeja; Ruler title: Jam Saheb; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1540; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Saurashtra (state)

name: Rewa State
label: indian princely states
description: Rewa State, historically known as the Kingdom of Baghelkhand, was the largest and wealthiest princely principality in central India's Bagelkhand Agency. Governed by the Baghel Rajput dynasty from their royal palace in Rewa, the state concluded a treaty of friendship and British protection on 10 May 1812. The maharajas held a seventeen-gun salute, administering extensive agricultural lands, mineral-rich forests and historical temples until the final ruler signed the instrument of accession to independent India in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state of British India; Capital: Rewa; Common languages: Bagheli and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely state; Ruling dynasty: Baghel; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1140; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Territory of Missouri
description: The Territory of Missouri was an organised incorporated frontier territory of the United States established on 4 June 1812 as the successor to the Louisiana Territory. Governed from the Mississippi River trade hub of St. Louis, the territory supervised extensive frontier settlements, westward expeditionary routes and burgeoning agricultural commerce across the central plains. Following the separation of the Arkansas Territory and the passage of the Missouri Compromise, its south-eastern core was formally admitted to the Union as the State of Missouri in August 1821. \n\n Status: Organised incorporated territory of the United States; Capital: St. Louis; Common languages: English and French; Religion: Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Territorial administration; Head of state: Governor; Historical era: American westward expansion; Established: 4 June 1812; Disestablished: 10 August 1821; Preceded by: Louisiana Territory; Succeeded by: State of Missouri

name: Bhaisaunda State
label: indian princely states
description: Bhaisaunda State was a minor princely estate located in the Bundelkhand Agency of central India, forming one of the prominent Kalinjar Chaube jagirs. Granted British confirmation through an official sanad in 1812 following the British capture of Kalinjar Fort, the estate was governed by hereditary Chaube Brahmins. Operating from the village of Bhaisaunda in modern Chitrakoot district, the rulers administered revenue collection and civil matters until the principality was integrated into the newly established state of Vindhya Pradesh in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state of British India; Capital: Bhaisaunda; Common languages: Hindi and Bundeli; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely estate; Ruling dynasty: Chaube; Ruler title: Jagirdar; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1812; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Dhurwai State
description: Dhurwai State was an autonomous princely estate located in the Bundelkhand tract of north-central India, originating as one of the historic Hasht-Bhaiya jagirs. Founded in the late seventeenth century by Diwan Rai Singh of the Orchha royal house, the estate maintained local feudal autonomy among neighbouring Bundela principalities during the twilight of Maratha dominance. Administered by hereditary diwans from the fortified village of Dhurwai, the polity preserved traditional clan governance until entering formal treaty arrangements with British authorities in the 1820s. \n\n Status: Autonomous princely estate; Capital: Dhurwai; Common languages: Hindi and Bundeli; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal jagir; Ruling dynasty: Bundela; Ruler title: Diwan; Historical era: Pre-Raj Central India; Established: 1690; Disestablished: 1824; Succeeded by: Dhurwai State (British Raj)

name: Kalinjar State
label: indian princely states
description: Kalinjar State was a historical princely estate situated beneath the formidable cliffside ramparts of Kalinjar Fort in the Bundelkhand region of modern Uttar Pradesh. Following the British reduction of the historic Chandela citadel in 1812, the British East India Company granted hereditary sanads to Chaube Brahmin commanders who had previously garrisoned the fortress. Administered from the ancient town of Kalinjar, the estate remained under the supervision of the Bundelkhand Agency until merging into the Indian Union upon independence. \n\n Status: Princely state of British India; Capital: Kalinjar; Common languages: Hindi and Bundeli; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely estate; Ruling dynasty: Chaube; Ruler title: Rao; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1812; Disestablished: 1949; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Kamta-Rajaula State
label: indian princely states
description: Kamta-Rajaula State was a small princely estate located within the Bagelkhand and Bundelkhand agencies of central India, situated near the sacred pilgrimage town of Chitrakoot. Established by a sanad granted by the British East India Company in 1812 to a family of Kayastha origin, the estate enjoyed revenue autonomy over several rural villages. The hereditary jagirdars managed local civil and judicial administration from Kamta-Rajaula until the principality surrendered its royal powers and joined the Indian Union in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state of British India; Capital: Kamta-Rajaula; Common languages: Hindi and Bundeli; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely estate; Ruler title: Rao; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1812; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Kingdom of Agwe
description: The Kingdom of Agwe was an autonomous coastal state established on the Bight of Benin along the borderlands of present-day Benin and Togo. Founded around 1812 by Ewe and Mina refugees escaping regional conflicts, the realm developed into a prominent maritime entrepôt for coastal transit, agricultural commerce and legitimate palm oil trade. Governed from the coastal port of Agoué, the monarchy preserved its political autonomy through diplomatic balances until French and German colonial partitions absorbed the territory into their respective protectorates in 1896. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Agoué; Common languages: Ewe and Gen; Religion: Traditional faiths and Christianity; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Precolonial West Africa; Established: 1812; Disestablished: 1896; Succeeded by: French Dahomey

name: Kingdom of Prussia and Russian Empire (Military Occupation)
description: The joint Prussian and Russian Military Occupation encompassed the contested German and Polish territories placed under combined allied administration following the retreat of Napoleonic forces in 1813. Directed by allied military commanders and central administrative councils, the occupation enforced requisitioning, recruited territorial militia and maintained civil order across the former Grand Duchy of Warsaw and central German principalities. This transitional wartime authority operated without a permanent capital until the final act of the Congress of Vienna partitioned Europe in June 1815. \n\n Status: Joint military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: German, Russian and Polish; Religion: Lutheranism, Eastern Orthodoxy and Roman Catholicism; Government: Allied military administration; Historical era: Napoleonic Wars; Established: 1813; Disestablished: 9 June 1815; Preceded by: Duchy of Warsaw; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Poland (Congress Poland)

name: Kolhapur State
label: indian princely states
description: Kolhapur State was a prestigious nineteen-gun salute Maratha kingdom situated in the southern Deccan plateau along the banks of the Panchganga River. Ruled by the senior branch of the royal Bhonsle dynasty tracing direct descent from Chhatrapati Shivaji, the realm concluded protective treaties with the British in 1812 to terminate maritime piracy and secure its frontiers. Administered from the historic palace city of Kolhapur, the state became renowned for pioneering social reforms and educational institutions before acceding to India in 1947. \n\n Status: Princely state of British India; Capital: Kolhapur; Common languages: Marathi; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Princely state; Ruling dynasty: Bhonsle; Ruler title: Chhatrapati Maharaja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1710; Disestablished: 14 August 1947; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Paldeo State
label: indian princely states
description: Paldeo State was a minor princely estate located in the rugged Bundelkhand Agency of central India, constituting one of the Chaube jagirs created after the fall of Kalinjar. Granted to a hereditary family of Chaube Brahmins by the British in 1812, the principality comprised eighteen villages spread over fifty-two square miles. Governed from the settlement of Paldeo near Nayagaon, the ruling raos directed rural agricultural development and local justice until merging into the state of Vindhya Pradesh in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state of British India; Capital: Paldeo; Common languages: Hindi and Bundeli; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely estate; Ruling dynasty: Chaube; Ruler title: Rao; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1812; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Taraon State
label: indian princely states
description: Taraon State was a small princely estate located in the Bundelkhand Agency of north-central India, forming another division of the historic Kalinjar Chaube jagirs. Established through a British sanad in 1812 following the pacification of the region, the estate encompassed thirteen villages surrounding the sacred Paisuni River. The hereditary jagirdars managed local land revenues and administrative matters from the town of Pathraundi near Taraon until the principality relinquished its ruling prerogatives to join the Indian Union in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state of British India; Capital: Taraon; Common languages: Hindi and Bundeli; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely estate; Ruling dynasty: Chaube; Ruler title: Jagirdar; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1812; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Tori Fatehpur
label: indian princely states
description: Tori Fatehpur was a princely estate located in the Bundelkhand Agency of British India, situated in present-day Jhansi district of Uttar Pradesh. Originating from the seventeenth-century partition of the Baragaon estate among the sons of Diwan Rai Singh, it constituted the largest of the Hasht-Bhaiya jagirs. The Hindu diwans governed several agrarian settlements from the town of Tori Fatehpur under British protection until the estate was dissolved and incorporated into independent India in 1950. \n\n Status: Princely state of British India; Capital: Tori Fatehpur; Common languages: Hindi and Bundeli; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely estate; Ruling dynasty: Bundela; Ruler title: Diwan; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1690; Disestablished: 1950; Succeeded by: Republic of India

name: Talysh Khanate
description: The Talysh Khanate was a semi-autonomous Caspian coastal realm situated between the Talysh Mountains and the south-western shore of the Caspian Sea. Facing persistent military incursions from Qajar Persia, Mir Mustafa Khan submitted to imperial Russian protection, confirmed in January 1813 following the Russian storming of Lankaran Fortress. Governed from Lankaran, the khanate served as a crucial Russian buffer state in the South Caucasus until direct imperial administration was imposed during the Russo-Persian War of 1826 to 1828. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the Russian Empire; Capital: Lankaran; Common languages: Talysh, Azerbaijani and Persian; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Hereditary khanate; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Caucasian Wars; Established: 13 January 1813; Disestablished: 1827; Succeeded by: Russian Empire

name: Guadeloupe
description: Guadeloupe during this brief interlude functioned as a Caribbean colonial possession of the Kingdom of Sweden during the latter stages of the Napoleonic Wars. Under the Treaty of Stockholm in March 1813, Great Britain transferred the island to Crown Prince Charles John, formerly Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte, as compensation for Swedish participation in the Sixth Coalition. Administered from Basse-Terre by British and Swedish representatives, the colony maintained its profitable sugarcane plantations until Sweden retroceded the island to Bourbon France under the Treaty of Paris. \n\n Status: Colony of the Kingdom of Sweden; Capital: Basse-Terre; Common languages: French, Swedish and Guadeloupean Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Colonial administration; Head of state: Charles XIII; Historical era: Napoleonic Wars; Established: 3 March 1813; Disestablished: 30 May 1814; Preceded by: British Leeward Islands; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France (Bourbon Restoration)

name: Crown Colony of the Island of Malta and its Dependencies
description: The Crown Colony of the Island of Malta and its Dependencies was a strategic British overseas territory situated in the central Mediterranean Sea. Established on 23 July 1813 when the civil protectorate was reconstituted as a crown colony under Governor Sir Thomas Maitland, British sovereignty was formally recognised internationally by the Treaty of Paris in 1814. Centred upon the fortified naval base of Valletta, the colony served as the headquarters of the Mediterranean Fleet until achieving independence in September 1964. \n\n Status: British crown colony; Capital: Valletta; Official languages: English, Maltese and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Crown colony; Ruler title: Governor; Currency: Maltese scudo and Pound sterling; Historical era: British Empire; Established: 23 July 1813; Disestablished: 21 September 1964; Succeeded by: State of Malta

name: Republic of Venezuela
description: The Republic of Venezuela, historically designated as the Second Republic of Venezuela, was re-established on 6 August 1813 following the triumphant conclusion of Simón Bolívar's Admirable Campaign. Proclaimed from Caracas, the republican administration attempted to reassert civilian authority and declared the Decree of War to the Death against Spanish royalists. Beset by ruthless counter-revolutionary assaults led by José Tomás Boves and royalist llanero cavalries, the republic fractured into regional factions before royalist forces under Pablo Morillo reconquered Venezuela in 1816. \n\n Status: Unrecognised revolutionary republic; Capital: San León de Caracas; Common languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Presidential republic; Head of state: Simón Bolívar; Ruler title: President; Historical era: Spanish American wars of independence; Established: 6 August 1813; Disestablished: 10 July 1816; Preceded by: Captaincy General of Venezuela; Succeeded by: Captaincy General of Venezuela

name: Duchy of Brunswick
label: german confederation
description: The Duchy of Brunswick was a sovereign north German state restored in October 1813 under Duke Frederick William following the expulsion of French occupation forces and the collapse of the Kingdom of Westphalia. Reconfirmed by the Congress of Vienna in 1815, the duchy became a member state of the German Confederation, administering its fragmented territories across Lower Saxony from the capital city of Braunschweig. The state introduced modern constitutional governance and industrialised railway commerce before joining the unified German Empire on 18 January 1871. \n\n Status: Sovereign state of the German Confederation; Capital: Braunschweig; Common languages: German and Eastphalian; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Welf; Ruler title: Duke; Currency: Thaler and Vereinsthaler; Historical era: German Unification; Established: 19 October 1813; Disestablished: 18 January 1871; Succeeded by: German Empire

name: Shamkhalate of Tarki
label: caucasian khanates
description: The Shamkhalate of Tarki was a historic Kumyk feudal principality occupying the Caspian littoral and foothill plains of modern Dagestan. Following centuries of autonomous rule under the hereditary shamkhals, the state was formally ceded to the Russian Empire under the Treaty of Gulistan in October 1813, retaining domestic feudal privileges as an imperial vassal. Administered from the ancient fortress town of Tarki, the shamkhalate functioned as an imperial administrative intermediary until Russian authorities abolished the domain in 1867. \n\n Status: Vassal domain of the Russian Empire; Capital: Tarki; Common languages: Kumyk and Russian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Tarki; Ruler title: Shamkhal; Historical era: Caucasian Wars; Established: 24 October 1813; Disestablished: 1868; Succeeded by: Russian Empire

name: Madisonville
description: Madisonville was a short-lived American naval settlement established on the island of Nuku Hiva in the Marquesas archipelago during the War of 1812. Founded in October 1813 by Captain David Porter of the frigate USS Essex, the outpost served to refit captured British whaling prizes and claim the island for the United States under the name Madison Island. Operating without a formal civilian administration from Fort Madison, the encampment was abandoned in May 1814 following escalating clashes with native Marquesan warriors. \n\n Status: Naval settlement of the United States; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: English and Marquesan; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Naval military encampment; Head of state: David Porter; Historical era: War of 1812; Established: 25 October 1813; Disestablished: 10 May 1814; Preceded by: Traditional Marquesan chiefdoms; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Taiohae

name: Kingdom of Spain and United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland (Military Occupation)
description: The joint Spanish and British Military Occupation comprised the territories of south-western France occupied by allied expeditionary forces during the final campaign of the Peninsular War. Commanded by the Marquess of Wellington, coalition divisions crossed the Pyrenees following the Battle of the Nivelle, capturing Bayonne, Pau and Toulouse. The allied commanders established provisional military logistics and civil oversight across Gascony without a formal capital until Napoleon's abdication and the Bourbon restoration brought hostilities to a close in April 1814. \n\n Status: Joint military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: French, English and Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Anglicanism; Government: Allied military administration; Head of state: Arthur Wellesley; Historical era: Napoleonic Wars; Established: 10 November 1813; Disestablished: 25 April 1814; Preceded by: First French Empire; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France (Bourbon Restoration)

name: Sovereign Principality of the United Netherlands
description: The Sovereign Principality of the United Netherlands was a transitional constitutional state established following the retreat of French imperial occupation forces in late 1813. Proclaimed in November 1813 by a provisional triumvirate in The Hague, the state invited Prince William Frederick of Orange-Nassau to assume hereditary sovereignty under a newly drafted constitutional charter. Administered from Amsterdam and The Hague, the principality successfully reorganised national finance, armed forces and civil administration before merging with the Southern Netherlands to form the United Kingdom of the Netherlands in March 1815. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: The Hague; Common languages: Dutch; Religion: Dutch Reformed and Roman Catholicism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Orange-Nassau; Established: 20 November 1813; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Netherlands

name: Radhanpur State
label: indian princely states
description: Radhanpur State was an eleven-gun salute princely realm located in north-western Gujarat, governed by the Babi dynasty of Pashtun ancestry. Formerly subordinate to the Mughal subahdars and later the Gaekwads of Baroda, the state concluded a treaty of subsidiary alliance and British protection on 16 December 1813 within the Palanpur Agency. Governed from the fortified trading city of Radhanpur, the nawabs fostered local agriculture, textile production and grain commerce until the final ruler acceded to the Indian Union in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state of British India; Capital: Radhanpur; Common languages: Gujarati and Urdu; Religion: Sunni Islam and Hinduism; Government: Princely state; Ruling dynasty: Babi; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1753; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Campbell Lands
label: boer states
description: Campbell Lands was an autonomous frontier settlement established in modern Griqualand West, South Africa, north of the confluence of the Vaal and Orange rivers. Formed by Griqua pastoralists, mixed-race frontiersmen and Korana clans under the leadership of Cornelius Kok II, the community maintained independence from the British Cape Colony. Centred upon the mission outpost of Campbell, named in honour of the missionary traveller John Campbell, the settlement preserved traditional captaincy governance until territorial reorganisations amalgamated the district into neighbouring Griqua domains. \n\n Status: Autonomous captaincy; Capital: Campbell; Common languages: Afrikaans, Dutch and Khoisan; Religion: Calvinism; Government: Traditional captaincy; Ruler title: Captain; Historical era: Precolonial South Africa; Established: 1814; Disestablished: 1 June 1824; Succeeded by: Waterboer's Land

name: Guler State
label: indian princely states
description: Guler State was a historic Rajput principality located in the Kangra valley of the Lower Himalayas in modern Himachal Pradesh. Originating as an ancient branch of the Katoch dynasty founded at Haripur in the fifteenth century, the state became celebrated across northern India as the birthplace of the refined Kangra style of Pahari miniature painting. Following the Anglo-Gorkha War, the British recognised the territorial rights and jagir revenues of the hereditary rajas, who maintained court traditions at Haripur until Indian integration. \n\n Status: Princely state of British India; Capital: Haripur; Common languages: Pahari and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely estate; Ruling dynasty: Katoch; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1415; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Maragheh Khanate
description: The Maragheh Khanate was a semi-autonomous vassal principality situated in southern Iranian Azerbaijan east of Lake Urmia. Ruled by the prominent Moqaddam Turkic tribal clan since the Safavid era, the realm maintained substantial hereditary authority under Qajar Persian suzerainty after the conclusion of the Treaty of Gulistan. Governed from the historic city of Maragheh, the hereditary khans commanded provincial cavalry contingents and managed regional agricultural revenues until modern centralising reforms by Reza Shah formally abolished the hereditary governorship in the 1920s. \n\n Status: Vassal state of Qajar Iran; Capital: Maragheh; Common languages: Azerbaijani and Persian; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Hereditary khanate; Ruling dynasty: Moqaddam; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Modern Iranian history; Established: 1814; Disestablished: 26 February 1916; Succeeded by: Sublime State of Persia

name: Sultanate of Asahan
description: The Sultanate of Asahan was a traditional Malay kingdom located along the north-eastern coast of Sumatra facing the Strait of Malacca. Founded in the seventeenth century as an offshoot of the royal house of Aceh, the sultanate flourished through its strategic riverine trade in timber, rattan and agricultural goods.
