name: Ascension Island
description: Ascension Island was formally occupied and garrisoned by the British Royal Navy on 22 October 1815 as a strategic outpost in the South Atlantic Ocean. Established initially to guard against potential French rescue missions targeting Napoleon Bonaparte on Saint Helena, the settlement centred upon the port of Georgetown. Over subsequent decades the isolated volcanic island evolved from an Admiralty station into a vital maritime refuelling depot and transoceanic communications hub. It retained colonial dependency status under the British Crown into the modern era. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Georgetown; Official languages: English; Government: Dependency under constitutional monarchy; Historical era: Late Modern period; Established: 22 October 1815; Currency: Saint Helena pound

name: United States of the Ionian Islands
description: The United States of the Ionian Islands was a federal aristocratic republic established under British protection following the Treaty of Paris in November 1815. Comprising Corfu, Cephalonia, Zante and four neighbouring islands, the state was administered by a British Lord High Commissioner alongside an elected Ionian Assembly and Senate. Although internal autonomy was exercised through local oligarchic institutions, British authorities retained decisive sway over foreign affairs and maritime defence. The protectorate was peaceably dissolved in May 1864 when Britain ceded the islands to the Kingdom of Greece. \n\n Status: British protectorate; Capital: Corfu; Official languages: Greek and English; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Federal oligarchy; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 9 November 1815; Disestablished: 2 May 1864; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Greece

name: United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves
description: The United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves was a pluricontinental monarchy created on 16 December 1815 when the Portuguese royal court elevated Brazil from colonial dependency to equal kingdom status. Governed from Rio de Janeiro until the royal family returned to Lisbon in 1821, the realm united vast transatlantic territories under the House of Braganza. Constitutional tensions between European and American elites culminated in Crown Prince Pedro declaring Brazilian independence in 1822. Portugal formally recognised the dissolution of the union and the sovereignty of the Brazilian Empire in August 1825. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Rio de Janeiro and Lisbon; Common languages: Portuguese; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Braganza; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 16 December 1815; Disestablished: 29 August 1825

name: Intermittent Guerrilla
description: Intermittent Guerrilla designates the dispersed insurgent networks that maintained resistance against Spanish royalist forces following the execution of José María Morelos in December 1815. Operating without a centralised capital or formal administrative apparatus, autonomous rebel bands under leaders such as Vicente Guerrero and Guadalupe Victoria fought across the rugged highlands of southern and central Mexico. These resilient partisan bands sustained the independence movement through regional ambushes and protracted defensive campaigns. Their prolonged defiance preserved the revolutionary cause until the proclamation of the Plan of Iguala in 1821. \n\n Status: Insurgent confederacy; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Decentralised military insurgency; Historical era: Spanish American wars of independence; Established: 22 December 1815; Disestablished: 24 August 1821; Succeeded by: Mexican Empire

name: AmaPondo
description: AmaPondo was an autonomous southern African kingdom situated along the subtropical Wild Coast between the Mtamvuna and Umtata rivers. Guided by hereditary paramount chiefs of the Nyawuza dynasty residing at Nyandeni and the Great Place, the Mpondo people maintained cultural cohesion and military independence throughout the turbulent nineteenth century. The realm successfully repulsed outside encroachments during the Mfecane and traded actively with colonial merchants while zealously guarding territorial autonomy. Pressure from imperial authorities escalated until Pondoland was formally annexed by the British Cape Colony in March 1894. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Nyandeni; Common languages: isiMpondo and isiXhosa; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Nyawuza; Ruler title: Paramount Chief; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Disestablished: 17 March 1894

name: Bilaspur State
label: indian princely states
description: Bilaspur State, historically remembered as Kahlur, was a prominent hill principality located along the Sutlej River in the lower Himalayas. Held by the Hindu Chandel Rajput dynasty, the kingdom accepted British paramountcy in 1816 following the conclusion of the Anglo-Nepalese War. Governed from the riverside capital of Bilaspur, the rulers administered their forested domain under the oversight of the Punjab States Agency. The state maintained its distinct political institutions until the reigning Raja signed the Instrument of Accession to the Indian Union in October 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Bilaspur; Common languages: Bilaspuri and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chandel; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: British Raj; Disestablished: 28 October 1948; Succeeded by: India

name: Hei-Khauan
description: Hei-Khauan was an autonomous Nama polity established across the arid plains of southern Namibia, centring its political authority at Berseba. Guided by hereditary leaders known as Kapteins alongside a council of elders, the community integrated pastoral traditions with Christian missionary influence while maintaining collective self-defence. The leadership navigated complex regional alliances with neighbouring Oorlam and Nama clans to safeguard grazing lands and communal independence. This indigenous self-governance endured until the territory was forcibly brought under imperial control by German South West Africa in 1896. \n\n Status: Traditional chieftaincy; Capital: Berseba; Common languages: Khoekhoegowab and Afrikaans; Religion: Christianity and traditional beliefs; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Kaptein; Historical era: Precolonial Southern Africa; Established: 1816; Disestablished: 1896

name: Kabadougou
description: Kabadougou was a powerful Malinké kingdom established in the savanna country of north-western Ivory Coast, centred upon the fortified commercial hub of Odienné. Founded by the warrior-statesman Vakaba Touré, the state flourished through control of vital trade arteries linking the forest belt to the upper Niger basin. Its leaders developed robust military cavalry and patronised Islamic scholarship while extracting tribute from surrounding agricultural communities. The kingdom retained its sovereignty until 1879, when it was vanquished and incorporated into the expanding Wassoulou Empire under Samori Touré. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Odienné; Common languages: Mandinka and Dyula; Religion: Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Touré; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 1816; Disestablished: 1879

name: Kumarsain State
label: indian princely states
description: Kumarsain State was a minor hill principality situated in the Shimla region of present-day Himachal Pradesh, overlooking the Sutlej River valley. Ruled by a lineage of Rajput thakurs, the realm suffered Gurkha occupation in the early nineteenth century before being reinstated under British protectorate supervision in 1816. The rulers exercised internal civil jurisdiction from the hereditary capital of Kumharsain while adhering to the diplomatic oversight of the Punjab States Agency. The principality preserved its traditional feudal structure until acceding to the Indian Union in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Kumharsain; Common languages: Pahari and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Rana; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1816; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: India

name: Kingdom of Oudh
label: indian princely states
description: The Kingdom of Oudh, traditionally known as Awadh, was an affluent princely realm occupying the fertile plains between the Ganges and Ghaghara rivers in northern India. Formally elevated to full royal status from a Mughal viceroyalty in the early nineteenth century, the Shia Muslim dynasty ruled from the grand cultural metropolis of Lucknow under British treaty obligations. While the kings cultivated renowned traditions of Urdu poetry, music and architecture, real strategic authority rested with the British Resident. In February 1856 the British East India Company deposed King Wajid Ali Shah and annexed the realm. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Lucknow; Official languages: Persian and Urdu; Common languages: Awadhi and Hindustani; Religion: Shia Islam and Hinduism; Government: Absolute monarchy under British protectorate; Ruling dynasty: Nishapuri; Ruler title: King; Historical era: British East India Company; Disestablished: 7 February 1856; Succeeded by: British East India Company

name: Neutral Moresnet
description: Neutral Moresnet was a miniature European condominium created on 26 June 1816 under the Treaty of Aachen to resolve border disputes between Prussia and the United Kingdom of the Netherlands. Encompassing valuable zinc deposits at the Vieille Montagne mine, the small triangular territory was governed jointly by two royal commissioners and a resident burgomaster based at Kelmis. Inhabitants enjoyed unusual legal privileges, including exemption from direct military conscription and minimal taxation. Following the Belgian Revolution, the Dutch administrative role was assumed by Belgium in 1831. \n\n Status: Condominium; Capital: Kelmis; Common languages: German, Dutch and French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Joint condominium; Historical era: Post-Napoleonic era; Established: 26 June 1816; Reorganised: 1831; Preceded by: First French Empire; Currency: French franc

name: Tristan da Cunha
description: Tristan da Cunha was formally annexed by the British Empire on 14 August 1816 when a military detachment was landed to prevent French rescue missions targeting Napoleon Bonaparte on Saint Helena. Perched in extreme isolation in the southern Atlantic Ocean, the settlement took root at Edinburgh of the Seven Seas as soldiers and civilian settlers established a communal farming and fishing economy. Over subsequent generations, islanders maintained self-governing traditions supported by an elected Island Council under British colonial protection. The dependency persevered as the world's most remote inhabited island community. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Edinburgh of the Seven Seas; Official languages: English; Religion: Anglicanism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Dependency under constitutional monarchy; Legislature: Island Council; Historical era: Late Modern period; Established: 14 August 1816; Currency: Pound sterling

name: Kingdom of the Two Sicilies
description: The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies was a sovereign monarchy established on 8 December 1816 through the formal unification of the crowns of Naples and Sicily under the Bourbon dynasty. Administered from Naples, the realm covered southern Italy and Sicily, forming the largest state in the peninsula prior to national unification. Its monarchs alternated between absolutist governance and short-lived constitutional concessions while suppressing frequent insurrections. The state collapsed during Giuseppe Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand and was formally incorporated into the Kingdom of Italy in March 1861. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Naples; Official languages: Italian; Common languages: Neapolitan and Sicilian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Bourbon-Two Sicilies; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Italian Risorgimento; Established: 8 December 1816; Disestablished: 20 March 1861; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Italy

name: Emirate of Ajman
description: The Emirate of Ajman was an independent maritime sheikhdom situated along the southern coast of the Persian Gulf, governed from the port town of Ajman. Led by the Al Nuaimi tribe, the emirate derived its livelihood from pearling, seafaring and coastal fisheries while maintaining strategic inland enclaves at Masfout and Manama. Its leadership fiercely defended local tribal autonomy against encroaching regional empires and neighbouring seafaring clans. Sovereign independence ended on 5 February 1820 when the ruling sheikh signed the General Maritime Treaty with the British Empire, entering the Trucial system. \n\n Status: Sovereign sheikhdom; Capital: Ajman; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Al Nuaimi; Ruler title: Sheikh; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Disestablished: 5 February 1820; Succeeded by: Trucial States

name: Grand Duchy of Hesse and by Rhine
label: german confederation
description: The Grand Duchy of Hesse and by Rhine was a sovereign German principality created within the German Confederation and administered from its ducal residency at Darmstadt. Ruled by the House of Hesse-Darmstadt, the state adopted its distinctive geographic designation in 1816 following territorial reorganisations that transferred Westphalia to Prussia in exchange for Rhenish Hesse. Grand Duke Louis I promulgated a progressive constitution in 1820, establishing a bicameral parliament that balanced conservative noble privileges with growing bourgeois liberalism. The grand duchy retained its sovereignty until joining the newly proclaimed German Empire on 18 January 1871. \n\n Status: Sovereign grand duchy; Capital: Darmstadt; Common languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism, Reformed and Roman Catholicism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Hesse; Ruler title: Grand Duke; Legislature: Landstände; Historical era: German Confederation; Established: 1816; Disestablished: 18 January 1871; Succeeded by: German Empire

name: Jaso State
label: indian princely states
description: Jaso State was a minor princely principality situated in the rugged Bundelkhand region of present-day Madhya Pradesh, bordered largely by Nagod and Ajaigarh. Governed by a branch of the Bundela Rajput dynasty from the fortified capital of Jaso, the state secured British imperial recognition through a formal sanad in 1817. Its rulers exercised hereditary revenue and magisterial powers over numerous rural agricultural settlements while acknowledging British paramountcy. The state retained its traditional dynastic administration under the Bundelkhand Agency until formally merging into the Indian Union in 1949. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Jaso; Common languages: Bundeli and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bundela; Ruler title: Diwan; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1817; Disestablished: 1949; Succeeded by: India

name: Möngpawn State
label: shan states
description: Möngpawn State was a traditional Shan principality situated in the scenic Nam Pawn river valley within the southern Shan highlands of eastern Burma. Ruled by a hereditary Saopha, the state functioned as a loyal tributary under the Konbaung dynasty of Burma while retaining full authority over local agricultural affairs. Its rulers paid periodic tribute in gold and silver to the royal court at Inwa and Mandalay and furnished military levies upon imperial summons. Burmese tributary suzerainty persisted unbroken until British colonial forces annexed Upper Burma in 1886. \n\n Status: Vassal state; Capital: Mong Pawn; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Konbaung dynasty; Established: 1816; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Möngsit State
label: shan states
description: Möngsit State was a compact upland Shan principality situated in eastern Burma, nestled among the forested ranges of the southern Shan plateau. Governed by a hereditary local ruler styled as a Myoza from the administrative centre of Möng Sit, the polity preserved traditional feudal governance beneath overarching Burmese suzerainty. The state fulfilled tributary obligations to the Konbaung monarchy, supplying ceremonial gifts and maintaining frontier order in exchange for royal protection. This vassal relationship concluded in 1886 when the British Empire dismantled the Konbaung kingdom and reorganised the Shan states. \n\n Status: Vassal state; Capital: Möng Sit; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruler title: Myoza; Historical era: Konbaung dynasty; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Sirmur State
label: indian princely states
description: Sirmur State was an influential Himalayan principality situated in the Giri River basin in present-day Himachal Pradesh, with its seat of government at Nahan. Governed by the Prakash dynasty of Rajput rulers, the state accepted British protection through a sanad in 1815 following the expulsion of Gurkha occupation forces. Sirmur enjoyed pre-eminent rank among the Punjab Hill States, fostering civic infrastructure, forestry management and iron foundry industries under progressive maharajas. The realm retained internal autonomy under British paramountcy until signing the Instrument of Accession to India in 1949. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Nahan; Common languages: Sirmauri, Western Pahari and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Prakash; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1815; Disestablished: 1949; Succeeded by: India

name: Soran Emirate
label: kurdish principalities
description: The Soran Emirate was a powerful Kurdish state centred upon the formidable mountain stronghold of Rawanduz in northern Mesopotamia. Under the energetic leadership of Mir Muhammad, known as the Blind Pasha, the revived emirate shook off Ottoman overlordship in 1817, expanding aggressively across neighbouring Kurdish valleys. The emir established armouries and mints, cast modern artillery and imposed rigorous central authority over regional tribal chieftains. Alarmed by his growing independence and territorial defiance, the Ottoman Empire launched a large-scale military expedition in 1837 that crushed the principality and restored imperial rule. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Rawanduz; Common languages: Kurdish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Mir; First ruler: Mir Muhammad; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 1817; Disestablished: 1837; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Zulu Kingdom
description: The Zulu Kingdom was a centralised southern African monarchy established along the eastern seaboard between the Tugela and Pongola rivers. Founded through the military innovations and political consolidation of King Shaka in the late 1810s, the realm integrated diverse northern Nguni clans into disciplined age-regiments. Operating from royal homesteads including Ondini, successive monarchs wielded absolute authority while guarding their independence against Boer trekkers and British imperial expansion. Following ferocious resistance during the Anglo-Zulu War, the kingdom was vanquished by British forces at the Battle of Ulundi on 4 July 1879. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ondini; Common languages: isiZulu; Religion: Traditional Zulu religion; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Zulu; Ruler title: Inkosi; First ruler: Shaka; Subsequent ruler: Cetshwayo; Historical era: Precolonial Southern Africa; Established: 1817; Disestablished: 4 July 1879

name: Alabama Territory
description: The Alabama Territory was an organised frontier dependency of the United States created on 3 March 1817 from the eastern section of the divided Mississippi Territory. Administered from the riverine settlement of St. Stephens by Governor William Wyatt Bibb, the territory oversaw rapid settlement driven by the post-war cotton boom. Its territorial legislature established judicial districts, surveyed fertile river valleys and prepared civilian institutions for statehood. Rapid demographic expansion enabled the territory to adopt a state constitution and gain admission into the Union as the twenty-second American state on 14 December 1819. \n\n Status: Organised incorporated territory; Capital: St. Stephens; Common languages: English, Muscogee and Choctaw; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Territorial administration; Ruler title: Governor; First ruler: William Wyatt Bibb; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 3 March 1817; Disestablished: 14 December 1819; Succeeded by: United States

name: Principality of Serbia
description: The Principality of Serbia was an autonomous Balkan state established under Ottoman suzerainty following the Second Serbian Uprising of 1815. Confirmed by imperial firmans under Prince Miloš Obrenović, the principality developed domestic self-governance, administrative ministries and a national assembly while transferring its capital to Belgrade. Serbian authorities maintained internal fiscal and judicial autonomy, though Ottoman garrisons continued to occupy key fortresses including Kalemegdan. This era of tributary vassalage culminated on 18 April 1867 when the last Ottoman military forces evacuated the Belgrade fortress, granting Serbia practical independence. \n\n Status: Vassal principality under Ottoman suzerainty; Capital: Belgrade; Official languages: Serbian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Constitutional principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Obrenović; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 26 July 1817; Disestablished: 18 April 1867; Succeeded by: Principality of Serbia (Sovereign)

name: Kingdom of Madagascar
description: The Kingdom of Madagascar was a sovereign island monarchy established through the rapid expansion of the Merina state under King Radama I. Formalised on 27 October 1817 via an Anglo-Malagasy treaty that recognised Radama as sovereign of the entire island, the kingdom ruled from the hilltop capital of Antananarivo. Merina monarchs and their powerful prime ministers modernised the army, adopted legal codes and embraced literacy and Protestant Christianity while resisting imperial encroachment. French invasion forces captured Antananarivo on 1 October 1895, deposing Queen Ranavalona III and converting the kingdom into a French protectorate. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Antananarivo; Common languages: Malagasy; Religion: Traditional Malagasy religion and Protestantism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hova-Andriana; Established: 27 October 1817; Disestablished: 1 October 1895

name: Kota State
label: indian princely states
description: Kota State was a major Rajput principality situated along the eastern bank of the Chambal River in the fertile Hadoti region of Rajasthan. Governed by the Hada Chauhan dynasty from the walled city of Kota, the state concluded a treaty of subsidiary alliance with the British East India Company on 26 December 1817. The realm achieved distinction as a seventeen-gun salute state celebrated for its distinctive school of miniature painting, imposing fortifications and prosperous riverine trade. Its hereditary maharaos governed under British paramountcy until signing the Instrument of Accession to India in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Kota; Common languages: Harauti and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hada Chauhan; Ruler title: Maharao; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 26 December 1817; Disestablished: 1950; Succeeded by: India

name: Emirate of Muri
label: fula jihads polities
description: The Emirate of Muri was a Fulani Islamic state established in 1817 along the Benue River valley in present-day north-eastern Nigeria. Founded by Hamman Ruwa during the religious campaigns of the Fula jihads, the emirate operated under the spiritual and political aegis of the Sokoto Caliphate. Its emirs governed multi-ethnic populations of pastoralist Fulani and indigenous agrarian communities from fortified settlements near the Muri Mountains. The emirate retained its regional autonomy until the Royal Niger Company and British colonial expeditions subjugated the territory at the turn of the twentieth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Common languages: Fula and Hausa; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic emirate; Ruling dynasty: Modibbo; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Fula jihads; Established: 1818; Disestablished: 1902; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Ilorin
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: Ilorin was an influential Islamic emirate situated on the frontier between the northern savanna and the southwestern forest zone of Nigeria. Originally a key provincial stronghold of the Oyo Empire, the city broke away in 1818 under the rebel general Afonja before transforming into an autonomous Fulani-led emirate under Shehu Alimi and the Sokoto Caliphate. The state wielded formidable cavalry power, reshaping regional politics across Yorubaland and fostering widespread Islamic learning and crafts from its walled capital at Ilorin. Its political independence ended on 5 March 1897 following defeat by the Royal Niger Company. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Ilorin; Common languages: Yoruba and Fula; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 1818; Disestablished: 5 March 1897; Succeeded by: Royal Niger Company

name: Karauli State
label: indian princely states
description: Karauli State was a venerable Rajput principality situated in the eastern reaches of Rajasthan within the cultural Braj region. Ruled by the Jadaun Rajput dynasty, who claimed direct descent from Krishna, the state accepted British protection in early 1818 through a treaty of subsidiary alliance. Governed from the fortified city of Karauli, the maharajas held ancestral estates along the Utangan and Chambal river ravines, patronising prominent Hindu temples and religious pilgrims. The state retained its traditional governance until acceding to the Indian Union and merging into the Matsya Union in July 1949. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Karauli; Common languages: Braj Bhasha and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jadaun; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1818; Disestablished: 4 July 1949; Succeeded by: Matsya Union

name: Republic of Venezuela
description: The Republic of Venezuela, historiographically designated the Third Republic, was a revolutionary South American state re-established by Simón Bolívar during the Venezuelan War of Independence. With the traditional capital of Caracas contested by Spanish royalist forces, the republican government operated primarily from the riverine bastion of Angostura along the Orinoco. Bolívar convened the historic Congress of Angostura in 1819, establishing constitutional principles, reorganising the patriot military and rallying international support. The republic was subsumed into the larger union of Gran Colombia through the Fundamental Law promulgated on 17 December 1819. \n\n Status: Revolutionary republic; Capital: Angostura (de facto), Caracas (de jure); Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Presidential republic; Head of state: Simón Bolívar; Historical era: Spanish American wars of independence; Established: 1818; Disestablished: 17 December 1819; Succeeded by: Republic of Colombia

name: Samthar State
label: indian princely states
description: Samthar State was an eleven-gun salute princely realm situated on the level agricultural plains between the Pahuj and Betwa rivers in Bundelkhand. Founded in the eighteenth century by the Bargujar clan, the state entered into a subsidiary alliance with the British East India Company in 1817. The ruling rajas exercised civil authority from the formidable ramparts of Samthar Fort, maintaining judicial and agrarian oversight of surrounding rural districts. The principality preserved its local autonomy under the Central India Agency until acceding to the newly independent Dominion of India following the end of British rule. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Samthar; Common languages: Bundeli and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bargujar; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1818; Disestablished: 1951; Succeeded by: India

name: Tamatave Kingdom
description: The Tamatave Kingdom was a coastal Betsimisaraka principality centred upon the vital eastern seaport of Toamasina on the Indian Ocean coast of Madagascar. Following King Radama I's successful eastern military campaign in 1817, the polity submitted to the suzerainty of the expanding Merina monarchy as a tributary vassal. Local leaders retained commercial autonomy and collected port duties while hosting foreign merchant establishments and facilitating trade between the central highlands and European naval powers. This period of vassalage terminated in 1829 when the Merina crown brought the coastal district under direct royal military governorship. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom; Capital: Toamasina; Common languages: Malagasy; Religion: Traditional Malagasy religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 1818; Disestablished: 1829; Preceded by: Betsimisaraka Confederation; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Madagascar

name: Tonk State
label: indian princely states
description: Tonk State was a seventeen-gun salute princely realm situated predominantly in Rajasthan, distinguishing itself as the sole Muslim-ruled principality in the Rajputana Agency. Founded by the Pashtun military commander Muhammad Amir Khan, the state was confirmed under British protection in late 1817 after Amir Khan agreed to disband his formidable mercenary forces. Ruled from the riverside capital of Tonk along the Banas River, the nawabs governed scattered territorial enclaves spanning Rajasthan and Malwa. The state preserved its distinctive Islamic legal and cultural institutions until acceding to the Indian Union in July 1949. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Tonk; Common languages: Urdu, Rajasthani and Hindi; Religion: Islam and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Salarzai; Ruler title: Nawab; First ruler: Muhammad Amir Khan; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1818; Disestablished: 4 July 1949; Succeeded by: India

name: Indore State
label: indian princely states
description: Indore State was a premier nineteen-gun salute Maratha principality governed by the Holkar dynasty in the Malwa region of central India. Following their defeat at the Battle of Mahidpur, the Holkars signed the Treaty of Mandsaur on 6 January 1818, ceding substantial outlying territories and placing their realm under British subsidiary protection. Administered from the bustling commercial and cultural capital of Indore, the maharajas promoted textile manufacturing, civic infrastructure and educational institutions. The state retained internal autonomy under the Central India Agency until acceding to the Indian Union following national independence. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Indore; Common languages: Marathi, Malvi and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Holkar; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 6 January 1818; Disestablished: 1950; Succeeded by: India

name: Sandur State
label: indian princely states
description: Sandur State was a Maratha princely principality situated in an iron-rich valley enclosed by the hills of modern Karnataka, governed from the capital of Sandur. Ruled by the Ghorpade dynasty, the state entered into formal subsidiary relations with the British East India Company on 7 January 1818 following the pacification of the Deccan. Supervised by the Madras States Agency, the rajas maintained local civil authority, oversaw rich mineral extraction and preserved traditional religious endowments. The principality concluded its separate political existence on 4 January 1949 by formally acceding to the Indian Union. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Sandur; Common languages: Kannada and Marathi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ghorpade; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 7 January 1818; Disestablished: 4 January 1949; Succeeded by: India

name: Udaipur State
label: indian princely states
description: Udaipur State, historically celebrated as the Kingdom of Mewar, was the premier Hindu princely realm of the Rajputana Agency, ruled by the prestigious Sisodia Rajput dynasty. Facing severe depletion from decades of Maratha exactions and internal factionalism, Maharana Bhim Singh concluded a treaty of subsidiary alliance with the British on 13 January 1818. Governed from the lake city of Udaipur, the maharanas enjoyed the highest dynastic precedence among the princes of Rajputana, cherishing centuries of martial defiance. The historic realm retained extensive domestic autonomy until joining the United State of Rajasthan in 1949. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Udaipur; Common languages: Mewari and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sisodia; Ruler title: Maharana; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 13 January 1818; Disestablished: 4 July 1949; Succeeded by: India

name: Bundi State
label: indian princely states
description: Bundi State was an ancient Rajput principality located within the rugged hills and fertile valleys of the Hadoti region in north-western India. Governed by the senior lineage of the Hada Chauhan dynasty from the hillside palace fortress of Bundi, the realm entered into a protective treaty with Great Britain on 2 February 1818. This alliance safeguarded the state from predatory Maratha raiding and restored stability to its agrarian revenue administration. The maharao rajas exercised hereditary rule under British paramountcy until signing the accession agreement that integrated Bundi into Rajasthan in July 1949. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Bundi; Common languages: Harauti and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hada Chauhan; Ruler title: Maharao Raja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 2 February 1818; Disestablished: 4 July 1949; Succeeded by: India

name: Republic of Chile
description: The Republic of Chile was established as a sovereign South American state on 12 February 1818, when Supreme Director Bernardo O'Higgins proclaimed formal independence from the Spanish Crown. Extending along a narrow geographic corridor between the soaring Andes Mountains and the Pacific Ocean, the young nation governed from its historic capital at Santiago. name: Republic of Colombia
description: The Republic of Colombia, historiographically known as Gran Colombia, was a vast South American republic founded on 17 December 1819 through the Fundamental Law proclaimed at the Congress of Angostura. Encompassing modern Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama, the union established its capital at Bogotá under the presidency of Simón Bolívar. The republic successfully completed the expulsion of Spanish imperial forces across northern South America and championed pan-American unity. Intense regional friction between centralists and federalists eventually fractured the union, leading to its formal dissolution on 19 November 1831 into three separate sovereign republics. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Bogotá; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Head of state: Simón Bolívar; Historical era: Spanish American wars of independence; Established: 17 December 1819; Disestablished: 19 November 1831; Succeeded by: Republic of New Granada, State of Venezuela and Ecuador

name: Korea State
label: indian princely states
description: Korea State, also designated Koriya, was a rugged hill principality located in the Chota Nagpur highland tract of modern north-western Chhattisgarh. Founded in the sixteenth century by the Chauhan Rajput clan, the state passed from Maratha overlordship to British protectorate supervision through an agreement signed on 24 December 1819. Governed from the town of Baikunthpur, the rajas administered extensive forests rich in coal and sal timber, governing rural Gond and Kol tribal populations. The principality preserved its hereditary autonomy under the Eastern States Agency until acceding to the Indian Union in 1949. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Baikunthpur; Common languages: Bagheli, Chhattisgarhi and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chauhan; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 24 December 1819; Disestablished: 1949; Succeeded by: India

name: Auchi
description: Auchi was an autonomous Afenmai city-state located among the rolling savannah-forest hills of northern Edo State in southern Nigeria. Organised into five traditional quarters under the spiritual and political leadership of the Otaru of Auchi, the polity maintained robust civic defence and judicial councils. Its inhabitants engaged in prosperous agricultural cultivation, iron forging and regional trade across the Kukuruku hills. The kingdom maintained its political independence and communal traditions against neighbouring imperial incursions until British colonial forces entered the region and imposed colonial protectorate administration in 1891. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Auchi; Common languages: Yekhee (Etsako) and Edo; Religion: Traditional religion and Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Otaru; Historical era: Precolonial West Africa; Established: 1820; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: Southern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Cutch State
label: indian princely states
description: Cutch State was a prominent seventeen-gun salute maritime principality occupying the coastal marshes and arid grasslands of the Gulf of Kutch in north-western Gujarat. Governed by the Jadeja Rajput dynasty from the fortified desert oasis of Bhuj, the kingdom entered into a subsidiary alliance with Great Britain in 1819 and 1820 following regional disturbances. The rulers, styled as Maharao, maintained maritime fleets, commanded salt and textile trade across the Arabian Sea and issued their own silver kori coinage. The state preserved internal sovereignty until acceding to the Indian Union in 1949. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Bhuj; Common languages: Kutchi, Gujarati and Sindhi; Religion: Hinduism and Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jadeja; Ruler title: Maharao; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1820; Disestablished: 1949; Succeeded by: India; Currency: Kutch kori

name: Mudhol State
label: indian princely states
description: Mudhol State was a nine-gun salute Maratha principality situated along the Ghataprabha River in present-day northern Karnataka. Governed by the historic Ghorpade dynasty from the capital of Mudhol, the state entered British protectorate relations in 1820 following the final collapse of the Maratha Confederacy. The rulers managed fertile irrigated lands, fostered weaving industries and maintained martial traditions renowned for the indigenous Mudhol hound. Administered under the Deccan States Agency, the principality retained extensive domestic authority until the reigning raja signed the Instrument of Accession to the Dominion of India on 3 August 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Mudhol; Common languages: Kannada and Marathi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ghorpade; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1820; Disestablished: 3 August 1948; Succeeded by: India

name: Trucial States
description: The Trucial States was a British maritime protectorate comprising a confederation of Arab sheikhdoms along the southern coast of the Persian Gulf. Initiated through the General Maritime Treaty of 5 February 1820 to suppress maritime raiding, the political order was consolidated through exclusive treaties with Great Britain. Local hereditary sheikhs maintained domestic tribal authority over their pearling ports and desert pastures while British political agents supervised maritime defence and foreign diplomacy from Abu Dhabi. The protectorate dissolved on 2 December 1971 when the constituent sheikhdoms federated to establish the United Arab Emirates. \n\n Status: British protectorate; Capital: Abu Dhabi; Official languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Confederation of traditional emirates under British protection; Ruler title: Political Resident; Historical era: Nineteenth to twentieth century; Established: 5 February 1820; Disestablished: 2 December 1971; Succeeded by: United Arab Emirates

name: Territory of Arkansas
description: The Territory of Arkansas was an organised incorporated frontier territory of the United States created by the formal spelling revision enacted on 21 April 1820. Initially governed from Arkansas Post, the territorial seat was permanently transferred to Little Rock in 1821 to accommodate growing inland settlement along the Arkansas River. The territory established a bicameral General Assembly, founded legal codes and oversaw extensive land surveying and plantation agriculture. Having reached the required population thresholds, the territory drafted a state constitution and was admitted to the Union as the twenty-fifth American state on 15 June 1836. \n\n Status: Organised incorporated territory; Capital: Little Rock; Common languages: English, Cherokee and Choctaw; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Territorial administration; Legislature: General Assembly; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 21 April 1820; Disestablished: 15 June 1836; Succeeded by: Arkansas

name: Liberating Expedition of Peru
description: The Liberating Expedition of Peru was a combined Chilean and Argentine military campaign organised to dismantle Spanish royalist power across South America. Commanded by General José de San Martín, the amphibious force sailed from Valparaíso and landed at Paracas Bay on 7 September 1820, operating from naval squadrons and mobile field headquarters without a civil capital. San Martín pursued a deliberate strategy of diplomatic isolation and tactical pressure that fractured viceregal resistance across coastal Peru. The expedition entered Lima in July 1821, culminating in the proclamation of Peruvian independence and the installation of the Protectorate. \n\n Status: Revolutionary expeditionary force; Capital: None (decentralised); Administrative seat: Mobile field command; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Expeditionary military command; Head of state: José de San Martín; Historical era: Spanish American wars of independence; Established: 7 September 1820; Disestablished: 21 July 1821; Succeeded by: Protectorate of Peru

name: Republic of Entre Ríos
description: The Republic of Entre Ríos was an ephemeral federalist state established in the Argentine Mesopotamia on 29 September 1820 by the regional caudillo General Francisco Ramírez. Encompassing the present-day provinces of Entre Ríos and Corrientes from its capital at Concepción del Uruguay, the republic was created to resist the centralist political hegemony of Buenos Aires. Ramírez styled himself Supreme Chief, enacting administrative regulations, organising postal services and assembling a disciplined provincial militia. Following Ramírez's defeat and death on campaign in mid-1821, the republic collapsed and was peaceably dissolved into regular provincial governance on 28 September 1821. \n\n Status: Unrecognised breakaway state; Capital: Concepción del Uruguay; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Presidential republic; Head of state: Francisco Ramírez; Ruler title: Jefe Supremo; Historical era: Argentine Civil Wars; Established: 29 September 1820; Disestablished: 28 September 1821; Succeeded by: United Provinces of the Río de la Plata

name: Free Province of Guayaquil
description: The Free Province of Guayaquil was a revolutionary coastal state created on 9 October 1820 when civic leaders in Guayaquil ousted Spanish colonial authorities. Guided by an emergency governing junta under José Joaquín de Olmedo, the maritime republic maintained authority across the littoral plains of western Ecuador. The administration secured regional harbours, proclaimed free commerce and raised patriot militias to defend coastal independence against royalist counter-attacks. This foundational phase concluded on 8 November 1820 when a provincial congress convened to promulgate a formal provisional constitution. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Guayaquil; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Provisional junta; Head of state: José Joaquín de Olmedo; Ruler title: President of the Junta; Historical era: Spanish American wars of independence; Established: 9 October 1820; Reorganised: 8 November 1820

name: Republic of Cuenca
description: The Republic of Cuenca was a short-lived revolutionary state proclaimed in the southern Andean highlands of Ecuador on 3 November 1820 following the outbreak of independence in Guayaquil. Centred upon the historic mountain city of Cuenca, patriot citizens and municipal leaders led by José María Vázquez de Noboa established a republican council and promulgated a liberal constitution. The young republic attempted to raise popular militias and secure mountainous mountain passes against approaching royalist columns from Quito. The state was extinguished on 20 December 1820 when Spanish royalist forces crushed the republican militia at the Battle of Verdeloma. \n\n Status: Revolutionary republic; Capital: Cuenca; Official languages: Spanish; Common languages: Quechua and Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Republican junta; Ruler title: President of the Council; Historical era: Spanish American wars of independence; Established: 3 November 1820; Disestablished: 20 December 1820; Succeeded by: Real Audiencia of Quito

name: Free Province of Guayaquil
description: The Free Province of Guayaquil entered its constitutional phase on 8 November 1820 following the formal adoption of its provisional electoral regulation. Governed from the vital port city of Guayaquil by a civilian triumvirate headed by José Joaquín de Olmedo, the maritime republic maintained sovereignty across the coastal littoral of modern Ecuador. The state maintained trade, levied customs duties and actively coordinated military operations with Colombian and Peruvian liberation armies. Sovereign independence ended in June 1822 when General Simón Bolívar arrived with Gran Colombian forces and annexed the province into the Republic of Colombia. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Guayaquil; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Constitutional republic; Head of state: José Joaquín de Olmedo; Ruler title: President; Historical era: Spanish American wars of independence; Established: 8 November 1820; Disestablished: 16 June 1822; Succeeded by: Republic of Colombia

name: Aundh State
label: indian princely states
description: Aundh State was a Maratha princely state situated among the rolling hills of the Deccan plateau in present-day southern Maharashtra. Ruled by the Brahman Pant Pratinidhi dynasty from the capital of Aundh, the estate came under British protectorate supervision in 1821 as one of the Satara Jagirs. The state achieved international renown in the early twentieth century for the pioneering Aundh Experiment, which instituted radical democratic village self-governance and grassroots swaraj. The principality preserved its progressive internal administration under the Deccan States Agency until acceding to the Indian Union on 3 August 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Aundh; Common languages: Marathi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Pant Pratinidhi; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1821; Disestablished: 3 August 1948; Succeeded by: India

name: Bemazava Kingdom
description: The Bemazava Kingdom was an autonomous northern Sakalava realm located along the fertile river estuaries and coastline of north-western Madagascar. Governed by hereditary Sakalava monarchs from their capital at Bemazava, the kingdom maintained independent maritime commerce with Swahili and European merchants while defending ancestral territories against encroaching Merina armies. The rulers mobilised warrior clans and coastal canoes to preserve regional sovereignty throughout decades of highland military pressure. This independent monarchical existence culminated on 14 July 1840 when Queen Tsiomeko sought French naval protection, ceding sovereignty over Nosy Be and adjacent coastal territories. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bemazava; Common languages: Sakalava Malagasy; Religion: Traditional Malagasy religion and Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Maroseranana; Ruler title: Monarch; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 1821; Disestablished: 14 July 1840; Succeeded by: French colonial administration

name: Boina Kingdom
description: The Boina Kingdom was a prominent western Sakalava realm along Boina Bay and the Betsiboka River in north-western Madagascar. Following sustained military campaigns led by King Radama I of Imerina, the monarch of Boina submitted as a tributary vassal in 1821 while preserving local dynastic courts. The Sakalava aristocracy collected maritime duties and administered regional trading networks with Arab and Swahili dhow captains under highland imperial surveillance. This tributary arrangement ended in 1841 when Merina forces occupied the kingdom directly, extinguishing Boina's royal autonomy. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom under Merina suzerainty; Capital: Boina Bay; Common languages: Sakalava Malagasy; Religion: Traditional Malagasy religion and Islam; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Maroseranana; Ruler title: Monarch; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 1821; Disestablished: 1841; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Madagascar

name: Bompey
label: english chieftancies in sierra leone
description: Bompey, historically known as the Bumpe Chiefdom, was an autonomous coastal and riverine polity situated in the Moyamba district of modern Sierra Leone. Centred upon the fortified trading settlement of Rotifunk on the Bumpe River, the realm was governed by hereditary Mende and Sherbro paramount chiefs. The chiefdom commanded lucrative regional commerce in palm oil, timber and piassava, balancing commercial treaties with British merchants in Freetown with indigenous customary law. Its independent existence terminated on 19 December 1881 when the paramount chiefs signed treaties ceding jurisdiction to the British Crown. \n\n Status: Sovereign chiefdom; Capital: Rotifunk; Common languages: Mende, Sherbro and Krio; Religion: Traditional beliefs and Christianity; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Paramount Chief; Historical era: Precolonial West Africa; Established: 1821; Disestablished: 19 December 1881; Succeeded by: Sierra Leone Colony and Protectorate

name: Gazikumukh Khanate
description: The Gazikumukh Khanate was a highland Caucasian principality inhabited principally by Lak and Avar communities in the mountainous interior of Dagestan. Subordinated to the Russian Empire in 1820 and 1821 following imperial campaigns in the Caucasus, the khanate retained internal self-rule under Russian-appointed khans residing at the mountain stronghold of Kumukh. Its rulers walked a perilous diplomatic line, balancing obedience to Russian imperial administrators against popular sympathies for the anti-colonial resistance led by Imam Shamil. The Russian government formally abolished the vassal khanate in 1860, incorporating its territory into the Dagestan Oblast. \n\n Status: Vassal khanate under Russian suzerainty; Capital: Kumukh; Common languages: Lak, Avar and Kumyk; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy under imperial protectorate; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Caucasian War; Established: 1821; Disestablished: 1860; Succeeded by: Russian Empire

name: Ibadan
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: Ibadan was a powerful Yoruba military state and oligarchic republic founded in 1821 as an armed camp following the decline of the Old Oyo Empire. Centred upon the sprawling fortified metropolis of Ibadan in south-western Nigeria, the state developed a unique meritocratic military government governed by councils of civil and military chiefs, styled respectively as Baale and Balogun. Ibadan field armies established hegemony over extensive Yoruba hinterlands through superior martial organisation and gun trading. Sovereign autonomy came to a close on 15 August 1893 when its chiefs accepted British protectorate terms. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Ibadan; Common languages: Yoruba; Religion: Traditional Yoruba religion and Islam; Government: Oligarchic military republic; Ruler title: Baale; Historical era: Yoruba Civil Wars; Established: 1821; Disestablished: 15 August 1893; Succeeded by: Lagos Colony

name: Miraj State
label: indian princely states
description: Miraj State, formally designated Miraj Senior, was an influential Maratha princely realm situated in the Krishna River valley of southern Maharashtra. Governed by the Patwardhan Chitpavan Brahman dynasty, the state was created as a distinct political entity in 1820 through the partition of ancestral Patwardhan estates and acknowledged under British protection in 1821. Ruled from the strategic railway and trading junction of Miraj, the rajas promoted agriculture, fine weaving and traditional Indian classical music. The principality preserved its domestic autonomy under the Deccan States Agency until acceding to the Indian Union on 3 August 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Miraj; Common languages: Marathi and Kannada; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Patwardhan; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1821; Disestablished: 3 August 1948; Succeeded by: India

name: Nagod State
label: indian princely states
description: Nagod State was an ancient Rajput principality situated in the modern Satna district of Madhya Pradesh, historically known as Unchahara. Held by the Parihar Rajput clan, the state entered into formal treaty relations with Great Britain in 1820 and 1821, securing imperial confirmation for its ancestral lands under the Bundelkhand Agency. Governed from the fortified settlement of Nagod along the Amran River, the rajas supervised agricultural revenue collection and maintained local law across numerous rural hamlets. The principality preserved its hereditary governance until formally merging into the Indian Union in 1950. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Nagod; Common languages: Bagheli, Bundeli and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Parihar; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1821; Disestablished: 1950; Succeeded by: India

name: Palanpur State
label: indian princely states
description: Palanpur State was a thirteen-gun salute princely realm situated in northern Gujarat, ruled by the Lohani Pashtun dynasty from the fortified capital of Palanpur. Following protracted regional instability, the diwans accepted British protectorate oversight in 1817 and 1821, leading to the creation of the Palanpur Agency. The rulers maintained civil and fiscal jurisdiction over a diverse territory bordering the Rann of Kutch, managing extensive cotton, grain and salt trade routes. The state retained its internal dynastic administration under British paramountcy until signing the Instrument of Accession to the Indian Union in 1949. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Palanpur; Common languages: Gujarati, Urdu and Hindi; Religion: Islam and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Lohani; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1821; Disestablished: 1949; Succeeded by: India

name: Singaling Hkamti State
label: shan states
description: Singaling Hkamti State was an outlying Shan principality situated along the upper reaches of the Chindwin River in the rugged highlands of north-western Burma. Ruled by a hereditary Saopha from the riverine settlement of Hkamti, the state operated as a loyal tributary to the Burmese Konbaung court following its foundation in 1820 and 1821. The rulers rendered periodic tribute in precious metals, forest products and jade while exercising customary authority over local Shan and Naga clans. Burmese suzerainty continued uninterrupted until British forces conquered Upper Burma and reorganised the frontier states in 1886. \n\n Status: Vassal state; Capital: Hkamti; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Konbaung dynasty; Established: 1821; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands
description: South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands was a sub-Antarctic maritime dependency of the British Crown located in the southern Atlantic Ocean. Claimed for Great Britain by Captain James Cook, the territory experienced organised British maritime administration and sealing activities from 1821 onwards. Operating under a colonial magistrate stationed at King Edward Point, the glaciated islands evolved into a major international centre for southern whaling stations and polar scientific exploration. The territory remained an overseas dependency of the United Kingdom into the contemporary era. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: King Edward Point; Official languages: English; Government: Dependency under constitutional monarchy; Historical era: Late Modern period; Established: 1821; Currency: Pound sterling

name: Wase Emirate
description: The Wase Emirate was a Fulani Islamic principality established in 1821 in the fertile savanna lowlands of present-day Plateau State in central Nigeria. Founded by Hassan, a Fulani warrior and scholar from Bauchi, the emirate emerged under the spiritual suzerainty of the Sokoto Caliphate, centring its administration at the foot of the dramatic Wase Rock. Its emirs governed a heterogeneous population of Fulani pastoralists and indigenous agrarian ethnic groups, promoting trade and enforcing Islamic jurisprudence. The emirate retained its regional autonomy until British imperial expeditions subjugated central Nigeria in 1899. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Wase; Common languages: Hausa, Fula and Tarok; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic emirate; Ruler title: Emir (Madaki); Historical era: Fula jihads; Established: 1821; Disestablished: 1899; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Hellenic State
description: The Hellenic State was the revolutionary republic established by Greek patriots on 17 March 1821 upon the outbreak of the Greek War of Independence against the Ottoman Empire. Initially guided by provisional assemblies, the state was centralised in 1828 under Governor Ioannis Kapodistrias, who instituted civil courts, national coinage and regular schools from the capital at Nafplio. Despite internal factional conflict and destructive Ottoman counter-offensives, the polity secured European diplomatic and military support. The state concluded on 21 July 1832 when the Treaty of Constantinople transformed Greece into an independent sovereign kingdom. \n\n Status: Revolutionary republic; Capital: Nafplio; Official languages: Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Presidential republic; Head of state: Ioannis Kapodistrias; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Greek War of Independence; Established: 17 March 1821; Disestablished: 21 July 1832; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Greece; Currency: Phoenix

name: Sultanate of Sennar
description: The Sultanate of Sennar was a historic Islamic realm along the Blue Nile in eastern Sudan that submitted to Ottoman-Egyptian suzerainty on 14 June 1821. Following the invasion dispatched by Muhammad Ali Pasha of Egypt, Sultan Badi VII surrendered his authority, reducing the ancient Funj monarchy to an imperial protectorate. Egyptian governors utilised the puppet sultans in Sennar to collect agricultural tribute and conscript local levies across the Gezira plains. This tributary protectorate ended on 13 February 1841 when Ottoman decrees formally incorporated the territory into the centralised administration of Egyptian Sudan. \n\n Status: Protectorate under Ottoman Egypt; Capital: Sennar; Common languages: Arabic and Nubian languages; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional sultanate under imperial supervision; Ruling dynasty: Funj; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Turco-Egyptian conquest; Established: 14 June 1821; Disestablished: 13 February 1841; Succeeded by: Ottoman Egypt

name: Protectorate of Peru
description: The Protectorate of Peru was a transitional sovereign administration established in Lima on 21 July 1821 under the leadership of General José de San Martín. Supported by Argentine and Chilean expeditionary armed forces, San Martín assumed the title of Protector of Peru, proclaiming national independence from the Spanish Empire and instituting foundational civil reforms. His administration created ministerial departments, abolished indigenous tribute, liberated children born to enslaved mothers and founded the National Library. San Martín voluntarily resigned his supreme authority on 20 September 1822, transferring sovereign executive power to the newly installed Constituent Congress of Peru. \n\n Status: Provisional protectorate; Capital: Lima; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Provisional military dictatorship; Head of state: José de San Martín; Ruler title: Protector of Peru; Historical era: Spanish American wars of independence; Established: 21 July 1821; Disestablished: 20 September 1822; Succeeded by: Republic of Peru

name: Mexican Empire
description: The Mexican Empire was a short-lived constitutional monarchy established on 24 August 1821 under the Treaty of Córdoba, securing independence from the Spanish Crown. Commanded by General Agustín de Iturbide, who was crowned Emperor Agustín I in July 1822, the vast empire spanned from California and Texas southward through Central America to the border of Gran Colombia. Governed from Mexico City, the imperial administration struggled with intense congressional opposition, depleted treasuries and regional republican uprisings. Iturbide abdicated on 19 March 1823, and on 1 April 1823 the imperial regime gave way to the Supreme Executive Power. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Mexico City; Common languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Iturbide; Ruler title: Emperor; First ruler: Agustín I; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 24 August 1821; Disestablished: 1 April 1823; Succeeded by: Supreme Executive Power of the Mexican Nation

name: Independent State of Spanish Haiti
description: The Independent State of Spanish Haiti was an ephemeral breakaway republic established on 1 December 1821 when José Núñez de Cáceres proclaimed independence from Spain in Santo Domingo. Terminating the colonial period known as España Boba, the new government promulgated a provisional constitution and sought diplomatic union with Simón Bolívar's Republic of Colombia. Lacking adequate military forces or foreign recognition, the infant state proved unable to withstand regional pressure. The republic was extinguished on 9 February 1822 when President Jean-Pierre Boyer arrived with Haitian forces, annexing the eastern part of the island into Haiti. \n\n Status: Unrecognised breakaway state; Capital: Santo Domingo; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Presidential republic; Head of state: José Núñez de Cáceres; Ruler title: President; Historical era: Spanish American wars of independence; Established: 1 December 1821; Disestablished: 9 February 1822; Succeeded by: Republic of Haiti

name: Changbhakar State
label: indian princely states
description: Changbhakar State was a compact princely realm situated among the rugged hills and dense forests of the Maikal Range in present-day Chhattisgarh. Governed by a lineage of Chauhan Rajputs from their administrative seat at Bharatpur, the state passed from Maratha overlordship to British protectorate supervision in 1822. The rajas exercised patriarchal authority over more than a hundred rural villages populated primarily by Gond and Baiga communities, managing forest timber and subsistence hill agriculture. The state preserved its internal governance under the Chhattisgarh States Agency until signing the Instrument of Accession to the Indian Union in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Bharatpur; Common languages: Bagheli, Chhattisgarhi and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chauhan; Ruler title: Bhaiya; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1822; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: India

name: Colony of Liberia
label: us colonies in liberia
description: The Colony of Liberia was a private settlement colony established on Cape Mesurado in 1822 by the American Colonisation Society to resettle free African Americans. Administered from Monrovia, named in honour of United States President James Monroe, the colony was directed by appointed colonial agents alongside immigrant town councils. The early Americo-Liberian settlers developed agricultural holdings and coastal trade while navigating complex relations and conflicts with indigenous Dei and Bassa chiefdoms. The colony expanded along the Atlantic seaboard until federating with neighbouring settlements to form the Commonwealth of Liberia in 1839. \n\n Status: Private chartered colony; Capital: Monrovia; Official languages: English; Common languages: Liberian Kreyol and indigenous languages; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Colonial administration; Ruler title: Colonial Agent; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 1822; Disestablished: 1839; Succeeded by: Commonwealth of Liberia

name: Gangpur State
label: indian princely states
description: Gangpur State was a forested princely realm situated along the valleys of the Ib and Sankh rivers in western Odisha. Governed by the Parmar Sekhar dynasty from the capital of Sundargarh, the state came under British imperial protection in 1822 following the pacification of the Maratha frontiers. The ruling rajas exercised domestic civil and judicial authority over a diverse population of Odia cultivators and indigenous Oraon, Munda and Kisan tribal groups. Supervised under the Eastern States Agency, the principality retained its traditional feudal governance until acceding to the Indian Union on 1 January 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Sundargarh; Common languages: Odia, Sadri and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism and traditional beliefs; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sekhar; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1822; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: India

name: Territory of Florida
description: The Territory of Florida was an organised incorporated territory of the United States created on 30 March 1822 through the consolidation of East and West Florida, acquired from Spain under the Adams-Onís Treaty. After rotating between St. Augustine and Pensacola, the territorial government established its permanent seat at Tallahassee in 1824. The administration expanded plantation settlement across the northern peninsula while fighting the protracted Second Seminole War against resistant indigenous clans. The territory concluded its twenty-three years of federal dependency when admitted to the Union as the twenty-seventh state on 3 March 1845. \n\n Status: Organised incorporated territory; Capital: Tallahassee; Common languages: English, Spanish and Mikasuki; Religion: Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Territorial administration; Legislature: Legislative Council; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 30 March 1822; Disestablished: 3 March 1845; Succeeded by: Florida

name: Empire of Brazil
description: The Empire of Brazil was a sovereign constitutional monarchy established on 7 September 1822 when Crown Prince Dom Pedro declared independence from Portugal. Governed from the coastal metropolis of Rio de Janeiro by Emperors Pedro I and Pedro II, the realm maintained political continuity and representative parliamentary institutions across a vast continent-sized territory. The imperial state fostered commercial expansion in coffee and sugar, triumphed in the Paraguayan War and abolished slavery through the Golden Law in 1888. The monarchy fell on 15 November 1889 following a military coup that proclaimed the First Brazilian Republic. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Rio de Janeiro; Official languages: Portuguese; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Braganza; Established: 7 September 1822; Disestablished: 15 November 1889

name: Republic of Peru
description: The Republic of Peru was established as a sovereign state on 20 September 1822 when the First Constituent Congress assumed authority in Lima following the resignation of José de San Martín. The young republic defeated remaining Spanish royalist forces through the decisive victory at Ayacucho in 1824, securing permanent South American independence. Governed from Lima, the state endured intense political rivalry among military caudillos while developing constitutional codes, mining revenues and coastal commerce. This initial constitutional era concluded on 15 August 1836 when Peru was partitioned and incorporated into the Peru-Bolivian Confederation. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital and largest city: Lima; Official languages: Spanish; Common languages: Quechua and Aymara; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Legislature: Constituent Congress; Historical era: Spanish American wars of independence; Established: 20 September 1822; Disestablished: 15 August 1836; Succeeded by: Peru-Bolivian Confederation

name: Agaie Emirate
label: fula jihads polities
description: The Agaie Emirate was an Islamic state established in 1823 in the fertile plains of the middle Niger basin in present-day Niger State, Nigeria. Founded by the Fulani religious scholar Malam Baba following the conquest of indigenous Nupe populations, the emirate operated under the spiritual and political suzerainty of the Sokoto Caliphate. Governed from the walled town of Agaie, its emirs promoted agriculture, collected regional tribute and deployed cavalry forces to protect commerce. The emirate retained its sovereign domestic institutions until 24 June 1898, when forces of the British Royal Niger Company subjugated the town. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Agaie; Common languages: Nupe, Fula and Hausa; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic emirate; Ruling dynasty: Baba; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Fula jihads; Established: 1823; Disestablished: 24 June 1898; Succeeded by: Royal Niger Company

name: Basoda State
label: indian princely states
description: Basoda State, also known as Haidargarh-Basoda, was a minor Muslim princely realm situated in the Malwa region of modern Madhya Pradesh. Founded in the eighteenth century by a scion of the Afghan Kurwai dynasty, the principality placed itself under British protection in 1822 and 1823 under the Bhopal Agency. Governed from the administrative headquarters of Haidergarh, the nawabs exercised internal civil and revenue jurisdiction over fertile black-soil agrarian tracts. The state preserved its separate dynastic autonomy beneath British paramountcy until the reigning nawab signed the Instrument of Accession to the Indian Union in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Basoda; Common languages: Urdu and Hindi; Religion: Islam and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Firoz Khel; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1823; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: India

name: Santiaogou Republic

description: The Santiaogou Republic was an autonomous Chinese kongsi federation of Hakka gold miners situated in the Monterado and Sepang districts of western Borneo. Operating under nominal Qing tributary allegiance, the miners seceded from the Heshun Confederation in 1823 to form an independent commonwealth directed by an elected council hall. The federation managed communal mines, collected commercial dues and maintained disciplined citizen militias to protect settlements against rivals. This democratic mining republic was dissolved in 1856 following military suppression by the Dutch East Indies colonial authorities during the Kongsi Wars. \n\n Status: Autonomous kongsi federation; Capital: Monterado; Common languages: Hakka Chinese and Malay; Religion: Chinese folk religion, Taoism and Buddhism; Government: Direct democratic kongsi republic; Legislature: General Assembly; Historical era: Kongsi Wars; Established: 1823; Disestablished: 1856; Succeeded by: Dutch East Indies

name: Supreme Executive Power of the Mexican Nation
description: The Supreme Executive Power of the Mexican Nation was the provisional government that administered Mexico after the collapse of the First Mexican Empire on 1 April 1823. Directed by an executive triumvirate including Guadalupe Victoria, Nicolás Bravo and Pedro Celestino Negrete from Mexico City, the regime dismantled imperial institutions and quelled provincial unrest. The administration accepted the peaceful secession of Central America while convening a constituent congress to draft a permanent republican framework. name: Federal Republic of Central America
description: The Federal Republic of Central America was a sovereign union established on 1 July 1823 following the collapse of Mexican imperial control over the region. Encompassing the constituent states of Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and later Los Altos, the federation governed initially from Guatemala City before relocating to San Salvador. The republic adopted an enlightened liberal constitution that abolished slavery and established a bicameral federal congress, yet suffered endemic strife between liberal federalists and conservative centralists. Devastated by civil wars, the federation disintegrated into separate independent nations, culminating in final dissolution in 1847. \n\n Status: Sovereign federal republic; Capital: Guatemala City and San Salvador; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Federal presidential republic; Head of state: Manuel José Arce; Ruler title: President; Legislature: Federal Congress; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 1 July 1823; Disestablished: 21 March 1847

name: Dhurwai State
