description: Dhurwai State was a minor princely jagir situated in the Bundelkhand region of modern Uttar Pradesh, forming part of the historic Hasht-Bhaiya group of estates. Derived from the partition of Orchha State among royal Bundela Rajput brothers, the domain was formally confirmed under British protection in 1823 and 1824 through the Bundelkhand Agency. Administered from the town of Dhurwai, the hereditary diwans collected agricultural revenues and settled local civil disputes across their rural villages. The estate preserved its dynastic institutions beneath British paramountcy until formally integrating into the Republic of India in 1950. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Dhurwai; Common languages: Bundeli and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bundela; Ruler title: Diwan; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1824; Disestablished: 1950; Succeeded by: India

name: Emirate of Afghanistan
description: The Emirate of Afghanistan was a sovereign Islamic state founded in 1824 when Emir Dost Mohammad Khan of the Barakzai dynasty established supremacy in Kabul following the collapse of the Durrani Empire. Operating from Kabul, the realm occupied a crucial strategic buffer between imperial Russia and British India during the Great Game. Afghan emirs mobilised tribal confederations to preserve national independence, triumphing in the First Anglo-Afghan War and maintaining Islamic legal governance. The emirate survived repeated imperial interventions until being elevated to the Kingdom of Afghanistan in June 1926. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Kabul; Official languages: Pashto and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Unitary Islamic emirate; Ruling dynasty: Barakzai; Ruler title: Emir; First ruler: Dost Mohammad Khan; Historical era: Great Game; Established: 1824; Disestablished: 9 June 1926; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Afghanistan

name: Foto
description: Foto was an autonomous Bamileke fondom situated in the Western Grassfields plateau of present-day western Cameroon. Governed by a sacred monarch titled the Fo from his ancestral palace complex near Bafoussam, the kingdom possessed intricate administrative structures supported by secret regulatory societies and titled lineage elders. The realm prospered through terrace agriculture, ironworking, artistic woodcarving and vibrant market trading across neighbouring highland valleys. Foto preserved its sovereign traditions and ritual autonomy against regional rivals until German imperial colonial forces established direct military control over the Bamileke plateau in 1901. \n\n Status: Sovereign fondom; Capital: Bafoussam; Common languages: Bamileke languages; Religion: Traditional Bamileke religion; Government: Sacred traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Fo; Historical era: Precolonial Central Africa; Established: 1824; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Sirohi State
label: indian princely states
description: Sirohi State was a venerable Rajput principality nestled among the southern Aravalli Hills and Mount Abu in south-western Rajasthan. Ruled by the Deora Chauhan clan from the capital of Sirohi, the state concluded a treaty of subsidiary alliance with Great Britain in 1824 to quell regional disorder. The realm was renowned throughout India for its skilled swordsmiths and celebrated Jain temple complexes, deriving stability through British protection. Administered under the Rajputana Agency, the state retained internal self-governance until acceding to the Indian Union in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Sirohi; Common languages: Marwari, Gujarati and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Deora Chauhan; Ruler title: Maharao; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1824; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: India

name: Sultanate of Mombasa
label: polities of the swahili coast
description: The Sultanate of Mombasa was an ephemeral British protectorate established on 8 February 1824 when Royal Navy officer William Fitzwilliam Owen accepted the submission of the ruling Mazrui clan. Seeking imperial protection against an impending invasion by the Sultan of Oman, the coastal elite hoisted the Union Jack over Fort Jesus. The provisional British administration oversaw harbour customs, monitored maritime trade and sought to suppress the local slave trade along the Swahili coast. The British government refused to sanction the arrangement, terminating the protectorate and withdrawing its garrison on 25 July 1826. \n\n Status: British protectorate; Capital: Mombasa; Common languages: Swahili and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional sultanate under British naval protectorate; Ruling dynasty: Mazrui; Ruler title: Liwali; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 8 February 1824; Disestablished: 25 July 1826; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Muscat and Oman

name: Sultanate of Johor
description: The Sultanate of Johor entered an era of British diplomatic influence following the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 17 March 1824, which divided the historic Johor-Riau realm into mainland and archipelagic spheres. Confined to the southern Malay Peninsula, the state was revitalised under the administration of the Temenggong family, who founded a new capital at Johor Bahru. The rulers modernised civil governance, attracted Chinese planters through the lucrative Kangchu agricultural system and expanded maritime commerce. This transitional phase culminated on 11 December 1885 when Great Britain formally recognised Abu Bakar as Sultan of an autonomous protectorate. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate under British influence; Capital: Johor Bahru; Common languages: Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bendahara-Temenggong; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 17 March 1824; Reorganised: 11 December 1885

name: Cornelis Kok's Land

description: Cornelis Kok's Land was an autonomous Griqua captaincy established across the arid plains of the middle Orange and Vaal rivers on 1 June 1824. Centred upon the mission outpost of Campbell, the state was founded by Kaptein Cornelis Kok II following a factional rupture with the leadership at Griquatown. The Griqua community governed through elected magistrates and mounted commandos, practicing pastoral agriculture and defending trade routes against neighbouring frontier groups. The captaincy retained its independent self-governance until internal successions and encroaching colonial claims brought its incorporation into Griqualand West in 1858. \n\n Status: Autonomous captaincy; Capital: Campbell; Common languages: Afrikaans and Khoekhoegowab; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Traditional captaincy; Ruler title: Kaptein; First ruler: Cornelis Kok II; Historical era: Precolonial Southern Africa; Established: 1 June 1824; Disestablished: 1858; Succeeded by: Griqualand West

name: United Mexican States
description: The United Mexican States, known historically as the First Federal Republic, was established on 10 October 1824 upon the promulgation of Mexico's first federal constitution. Administered from Mexico City, the federation united nineteen states and four territories under the inaugural presidency of Guadalupe Victoria. Despite establishing representative congresses and national judicial institutions, the republic suffered severe political instability caused by bitter conflict between liberal federalists and conservative centralists. The federal structure was overturned on 23 October 1835 when conservatives under Antonio López de Santa Anna established the Centralist Republic of Mexico. \n\n Status: Sovereign federal republic; Capital: Mexico City; Common languages: Spanish and indigenous languages; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Federal presidential republic; Established: 10 October 1824; Disestablished: 23 October 1835; Succeeded by: Centralist Republic of Mexico

name: Emirate of Nejd
description: The Emirate of Nejd, historically designated the Second Saudi State, was an Islamic monarchy restored across central Arabia in 1825 by Imam Turki bin Abdullah Al Saud. Operating from the new capital of Riyadh, the dynasty reasserted authority across Nejd and the Persian Gulf littoral following the devastating Ottoman-Egyptian invasion. The emirs governed through strict Hanbali Islamic jurisprudence, uniting bedouin tribes and oasis settlements under their political and religious banner. Severe dynastic infighting eventually undermined the state, leading to its conquest by the Rashidi Emirate of Jabal Shammar in January 1891. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Riyadh; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Saud; Established: 1825; Disestablished: 24 January 1891

name: Gaza Empire

description: The Gaza Empire was a powerful southern African military realm founded in 1825 by the Nguni general Soshangane during the regional migrations of the Mfecane. Controlling the vast lowlands between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers in southern Mozambique, the empire ruled from its capital at Manjacaze. The Gaza monarchs integrated diverse Tsonga and Ndau populations into disciplined age-regiments, commanding substantial tributary wealth and ivory commerce. The empire maintained its independence until 7 November 1895, when Portuguese colonial armies defeated King Ngungunhane and dismantled the state. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Manjacaze; Common languages: Nguni and Tsonga; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Nxumalo; Established: 1825; Disestablished: 7 November 1895

name: Kingdom of Nxaba

description: The Kingdom of Nxaba was an independent Nguni state established along the Save River basin in central Mozambique in 1825 by the military leader Nxaba Msane. Having migrated northwards from coastal southern Africa during the Mfecane, Nxaba organised indigenous Shona and Ndau populations beneath his centralised military command at Save. The kingdom deployed disciplined warrior regiments to defend rich riverine pastures and secure regional trading corridors. This martial realm was extinguished in 1838 when the superior armies of Soshangane's expanding Gaza Empire routed Nxaba's forces and annexed his domains. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Save; Common languages: Nguni and Shona; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Military monarchy; Ruler title: King; First ruler: Nxaba Msane; Historical era: Precolonial Southern Africa; Established: 1825; Disestablished: 1838; Succeeded by: Gaza Empire

name: Kingdom of Vientiane
description: The Kingdom of Vientiane was a historic Lao realm along the Mekong River that existed as a tributary vassal under the suzerainty of the Siamese Rattanakosin Kingdom. Governed from the riverside royal capital of Vientiane by King Anouvong, the state paid triennial tribute in golden and silver trees while retaining domestic Buddhist institutions. Tensions over Siamese labour corvée and sovereign subordination drove King Anouvong to launch a widespread war of liberation in late 1826. Siamese armies thoroughly defeated the Lao forces, capturing the king, destroying Vientiane and formally annexing the kingdom into Siam in 1829. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom under Siamese suzerainty; Capital: Vientiane; Common languages: Lao; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Vientiane; Ruler title: King; First ruler: Anouvong; Historical era: Rattanakosin era; Established: 1825; Disestablished: 1829; Succeeded by: Rattanakosin Kingdom (Siam)

name: Lafiagi Emirate

description: The Lafiagi Emirate was an Islamic state established in 1825 along the southern banks of the Niger River in modern Kwara State, Nigeria. Founded by Mallam Maliki, a Fulani scholar affiliated with the Sokoto Caliphate, the emirate consolidated control over local Nupe communities from its seat at Lafiagi. Its emirs fostered extensive floodplain agriculture in rice and sugarcane while managing regional commercial traffic across the Niger waterway. The emirate preserved its sovereign political institutions until British colonial forces subjugated the region and imposed colonial protectorate administration in 1901. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Lafiagi; Common languages: Nupe, Fula and Hausa; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Fula jihads; Established: 1825; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Manipur State
label: indian princely states
description: Manipur State was a historic princely kingdom situated in the Imphal Valley along the frontier between north-eastern India and Burma. Following the expulsion of Burmese invaders with British assistance, Raja Gambhir Singh established a protective subsidiary alliance in 1825. Governed from the Kangla Palace in Imphal, the Hindu Meitei monarchs preserved distinct judicial codes, royal polo traditions and classical dance under the Assam Agency. The kingdom maintained its internal autonomy under British paramountcy until signing the Instrument of Accession to the Dominion of India on 15 August 1947. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Imphal; Common languages: Meitei (Manipuri); Religion: Vaishnavite Hinduism and Sanamahism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ningthouja; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1825; Disestablished: 15 August 1947; Succeeded by: India

name: Massina Empire

description: The Massina Empire, also known as the Caliphate of Hamdullahi, was a Fulani theocratic state situated in the Inner Niger Delta of central Mali. Founded during the Islamic jihads by Seku Amadu, the caliphate was directed from the religious capital of Hamdallaye. Governed by a supreme Almami alongside a Grand Council of Muslim jurists, the state regulated transhumant cattle routes, settled pastoralist clans and enforced rigorous sharia jurisprudence. The empire retained sovereign hegemony across the middle Niger until 16 May 1862, when it was vanquished and annexed by the Toucouleur Empire under Umar Tall. \n\n Status: Sovereign caliphate; Capital: Hamdallaye; Common languages: Fula (Maasina Fulfulde); Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic theocracy; Ruling dynasty: Bari; Established: 1825; Disestablished: 16 May 1862

name: New Georgia
label: us colonies in liberia
description: New Georgia was a specialised settlement colony established in 1825 along Stockton Creek north of Monrovia under the auspices of the American Colonisation Society. Populated primarily by recaptives—Africans liberated from illicit slave vessels by the United States Navy—the settlement was organised into a productive agrarian community governed under colonial regulations. The settlers cultivated rice, cassavas and vegetables, supplying essential provisions to Monrovia while serving as an armed militia protecting the colonial frontier. New Georgia maintained its distinct communal identity under colonial agent oversight until merging into the Commonwealth of Liberia on 1 April 1839. \n\n Status: Settlement colony of the American Colonisation Society; Capital: Monrovia; Official languages: English; Common languages: Liberian Kreyol and West African languages; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Colonial administration; Ruler title: Colonial Agent; Historical era: Nineteenth century; Established: 1825; Disestablished: 1 April 1839; Succeeded by: Commonwealth of Liberia
